fullText:
NEW YORK, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Republicans are pouring money into more than three dozen US House races previously considered "safe" after internal polling showed they could be vulnerable in the November 3 election, according to three Republican operatives familiar with the party's thinking.

The shift is already starting to show in advertising reservations and campaign finance filings. Since September 1, major Republican groups and megadonors have begun ‌spending in at least 39 congressional races where they haven't previously deployed money this cycle, a Reuters review of spending by some of the largest Republican political groups shows.

Many of the candidates receiving new support ‌sit in Republican strongholds and are still running ahead of Democratic opponents in public polls, these people said, indicating rising worry among party leaders over whether voters will use the November 3 election to air dissatisfaction over US President Donald Trump's policies.

House Republican leaders recently warned dozens of ​campaigns that the party's internal data shows that they cannot assume they will win, even if they are currently ahead in public polls and represent districts Trump won by double digits, two of the people said.

"Republicans are playing defense in some of the strongholds that they're used to not having to worry about," said Republican strategist Ron Bonjean, a partner at bipartisan public affairs firm Rokk Solutions.

Republicans currently hold a narrow 218-214 majority in the House, with one independent caucusing with Republicans and two vacancies. Democrats would need to net at least four seats in the midterms to take control of the chamber next year.

Two Republican operatives working with party leaders said they're using their larger spending power to stifle Democrats before they ‌have a chance to attack. They said the party was taking out "insurance policies" ⁠to ensure Republican-held districts remain in the party's hands.

"Republicans are deploying our massive war chest to drive voters to the polls and supercharge our candidates," said Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee. "We're not taking anything for granted, because, unlike Democrats, Republicans aren't throwing in the towel on races we can win."

Republican Representative Bryan Steil is one telling ⁠example. His Wisconsin district voted for Trump by about 4.5 percentage points in 2024 and is rated "lean Republican" by Cook Political Report. Still, conservative super PACs dumped $1.5 million on his race this month, their first investment of this election cycle. A representative for Steil declined to comment.

In North Carolina's 3rd Congressional District east of Raleigh, Representative Gregory Murphy this month received $131,107 from a conservative PAC a week ago – the first outside spending on his behalf in the midterms. Democrats have spent over $326,000 trying to oust him since ​July. ​Trump won the district by 14 percentage points and Cook rates it "solid Republican." Murphy's office didn't return a request for comment.

The emergency ​deployments reflect a harsh reality: economic strain is battering traditionally Republican strongholds. Rising gas prices, ‌energy costs and fertilizer expenses are hitting voters in the agricultural heartland particularly hard.

One Republican House campaign aide said the environment for candidates in Iowa, Kansas and other Midwest states was "dire" as diesel prices soar.

"We're in this crucial period in the last 30 days where candidates have to really make a case, given how tough the headwinds are," said Kevin Madden, who advised former Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney and is now senior partner at corporate advisory firm Penta Group. Campaigns are running as if they are behind in the polls "even in red districts or traditionally safe" ones, Madden said.

More than $1.56 billion, overall, has been spent by independent committees on federal elections so far, with roughly $496 million deployed just since Labor Day, according to a Reuters analysis of super PAC spending. That figure doesn't include all spending by dark money nonprofits that do not disclose their donors.

Republicans have reserved at least $888 million in advertising over the coming weeks, compared ‌to at least $666 million for Democrats, according to AdImpact, which tracks political advertising. No Going Back PAC, which is fully funded by ​Trump's super PAC MAGA Inc., is leading the surge, Federal Election Commission records show.

"That's the advantage of having a shit ton of money," ​said one Republican operative working on Trump's midterm strategy. "We're not going to let Democrats take free shots on ​goal."

Over the last three weeks through Frday, Republican-leaning super PACs have outspent Democrats by almost 2-to-1, showering races with roughly $309.7 million since Labor Day compared with $174.2 million going to help Democratic ‌candidates, the FEC data shows.

"Republicans have air superiority. House Democrats are scrambling to catch ​up with the very limited resources they have," said Mike ​Marinella, national press secretary for the National Republican Congressional Committee, which works to elect Republicans to the House.

Democrats acknowledge their funding disadvantage but say the Republican push to spend money on districts that Trump won easily reflects the trouble the party faces in the midterms.

"Republicans are running scared, know they've lost the American people, and are trying one last hail mary to spend their way out of certain defeat," said Viet ​Shelton, spokesman for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

In one district in south Texas that Trump won ‌by 18 percentage points in 2024, Republican groups have pumped about $2 million into text messages, direct mail and digital ads since September 5 to help incumbent Representative Monica De La Cruz keep her seat. Cook Political ​Report moved her seat from "lean Republican" to "tossup" on Friday.

De La Cruz is grateful for her supporters helping defeat her rival, her campaign manager said, when asked about the money spent by her ​Republican backers.

title: Nor'easter floods the coast, leaving 1 man dead and thousands without power
description:
A slow-moving nor'easter continued to batter the Northeast on Sunday, bringing more rain, strong winds and another round of coastal flooding after a weekend that killed at least one person.
A New York City Housing Authority employee died Saturday afternoon after a tree fell on him in East New York, Brooklyn, CBS News reported. fullText:
A slow-moving nor'easter continued to batter the Northeast on Sunday, bringing more rain, strong winds and another round of coastal flooding after a weekend that killed at least one person.

A New York City Housing Authority employee died Saturday afternoon after a tree fell on him in East New York, Brooklyn, CBS News reported. A man who had been reported missing after he was seen swimming off Fire Island on Saturday contacted police Sunday morning and was found unharmed, state police said.

About 136,000 homes and businesses were without power across New Jersey, New York, Connecticut, Massachusetts and Rhode Island as of Sunday morning, according to PowerOutage.us, up from about 85,000 on Saturday. Ocean and Monmouth counties in New Jersey and Suffolk County on Long Island were among the hardest hit.

The storm was drifting near the New Jersey coast Sunday morning and is expected to ease Sunday afternoon before moving away late Monday, according to the National Weather Service. Minor to moderate coastal flooding was expected with Sunday morning's high tide, and gusts of 40 to 50 mph remained possible from New Jersey to Long Island. More than 6 inches of rain had fallen in parts of southeastern Massachusetts and about 5 inches along the northern Jersey Shore.

Never drive or walk through floodwaters. Just 6 inches of moving water can knock a person down.

Move cars out of flood-prone areas before high tide.

If you live in a basement or ground-floor apartment, have more than one way out.

Stay away from downed power lines and report them to your utility or 911.

In New York City, text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 for emergency alerts.

Follow below for the latest updates.

People in flooded coastal neighborhoods of New York and New Jersey took to kayaks and canoes over the weekend, paddling down streets past cars sitting in deep water, CBS News reported.

In Howard Beach, Queens, water ranged from several inches to more than a foot deep Saturday, according to CBS New York. A video posted by a storm chaser that morning showed two people paddling to the entrance of the Howard Beach–JFK Airport station, and it had drawn millions of views on X.

Water at Kings Point, N.Y., on western Long Island Sound, reached about 3 feet above the normal high-tide mark just after 11 a.m. Sunday and was still rising, according to preliminary NOAA data. That's already higher than the gauge reached with Saturday night's tide.

NYC Emergency Management had warned that the midday tide could bring moderate flooding to the coastal Bronx and northern Queens, including parts of Flushing and Astoria.

The hurricane watch and tropical storm warning for Hawaii's Big Island have been lifted, and there are no coastal watches or warnings in effect for the islands, according to the Central Pacific Hurricane Center. As of 11 p.m. HST Saturday, Nolo was about 200 miles south-southwest of South Point, moving west at 9 mph with 100 mph winds. It is still expected to become a major hurricane Sunday or Sunday night but stay well south of the main islands.

Emergency crews in Sea Bright, N.J., rescued a woman and her dog after their car became trapped in floodwaters, ABC7 reported, according to the Associated Press. In Surf City, a marina owner said customers reported boats and Jet Skis missing or blown off their lifts.

Farther south, flooding cut off highway access to North Carolina's Hatteras Island, stranding visitors, the AP reported.

Water at Sandy Hook, N.J., reached about 3.3 feet above the normal high-tide mark shortly after 9 a.m. Sunday, nearly matching Saturday's peak, according to preliminary NOAA data. At the Battery in Lower Manhattan, water rose to about 2.9 feet above normal around 9:45 a.m., and Atlantic City reached about 2.8 feet.

NYC Emergency Management had warned that Sunday's midday tide could bring moderate flooding to the coastal Bronx and northern Queens, including parts of Flushing and Astoria.

Rain totals climbed overnight, with the heaviest amounts in southeastern Massachusetts and along the northern Jersey Shore, according to National Weather Service reports.

A volunteer observer north of New Bedford, Mass., measured 6.47 inches by Sunday morning, and Bridgewater, Mass., recorded more than 5 inches, according to the NWS in Boston. In New Jersey, Bradley Beach recorded about 5.1 inches and Long Branch about 4.4 inches, according to the NWS in Mount Holly. On Long Island, East Hampton and Southold recorded more than 3 inches, as did Howard Beach in Queens, the NWS in New York reported.

Up to 2 to 4 more inches are possible in parts of coastal New Jersey and New England through Monday, ABC News reported.

About 136,000 customers were without power across five Northeast states as of about 10:30 a.m. Sunday, according to PowerOutage.us, up sharply from Saturday.

New Jersey had about 57,700 outages, including more than 24,000 in Ocean County and 13,000 in Monmouth County. New York had about 36,300, with nearly 18,500 in Suffolk County. Connecticut had about 29,200 and Massachusetts about 11,300.

A 56-year-old New York City Housing Authority employee died Saturday after a tree fell on him near the Cypress Hills Houses in East New York, Brooklyn, CBS New York reported. Police said he was taken to a hospital around 3:30 p.m. and died of his injuries. CBS News identified him as Leighton Brown.

A man who had been the subject of a search after he was seen swimming in rough surf off Robert Moses State Park on Fire Island on Saturday was located alive and uninjured Sunday morning, New York State Police said. Police said the man contacted them after seeing news coverage of the search.

Most of Long Island and New York City had received 1 to 2 inches of rain by Saturday afternoon, according to National Weather Service reports. A weather station in Long Beach, N.Y., recorded 2.27 inches, one of the highest totals in the region. The NWS office in Upton, N.Y., measured 1.85 inches, and JFK Airport had 1.27 inches.

Forecasters expect the heaviest rain overnight. City officials said bands of rain falling at up to 1 inch an hour are expected from about 8 p.m. Saturday into Sunday morning, with some neighborhoods getting 2 to 3 inches more.

Emergency workers evacuated about 20 people from a waterfront Comfort Inn in Edgewater, N.J., on Saturday morning after its first floor flooded, and were going back for more, The New York Times reported.

Federal air traffic officials warned that ground stops or delays are possible Saturday evening at the three major airports serving New York City, according to an FAA advisory. Boston Logan remains the hardest hit so far, with about a quarter of its flights canceled.

Amtrak has also canceled several trains, including service between Connecticut and Massachusetts and some trains between Boston and Philadelphia, citing weather and downed wires.

Along with the Global Citizen Festival and Ed Sheeran's Gillette Stadium shows, organizers across the region have canceled or rescheduled events because of the storm:

AC/DC's Friday concert at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J., was postponed to Oct. 2, the stadium said.

All Things Go, a three-day music festival in New York City, was canceled, with refunds offered.

Saturday's Yankees-Orioles game was moved to a Friday doubleheader, and tickets can be exchanged.

An Ironman triathlon at Jones Beach was canceled.

Horse racing at Belmont Park was canceled Saturday and Sunday, the New York Racing Association said.

The New York Renaissance Faire in Tuxedo Park is closed for the weekend, with automatic refunds, organizers said.

Water levels along the New York and New Jersey coast fell well below their morning peaks by early Saturday afternoon, according to NOAA tide gauges. At the Battery in Lower Manhattan, the water dropped more than 5 feet from its 9:36 a.m. peak by just after 2 p.m.

However, the drop is temporary. The next high tide is expected around 8:15 to 9 p.m. along the city's south shore and near midnight along Long Island Sound, according to NYC Emergency Management, with moderate flooding expected again in Jamaica Bay and the Rockaways. Forecasters have said the heaviest rain in the city will also arrive tonight, which could slow drainage in low-lying areas.

PSEG Long Island said Saturday morning that it had restored power to more than 23,000 customers since 7 a.m. Friday, and that more than 850 line workers, tree trimmers and other field staff were responding, according to a storm update. The utility said the hardest-hit areas were the Town of Huntington and the South Shore of western Suffolk County.

PSEG Long Island warned that more outages are likely as the wind and rain continue, and that strong winds could temporarily slow repairs because crews can't safely work in bucket trucks in high gusts.

Floodwater swept through the streets of Surf City, N.J., on Saturday and got into some homes, the Associated Press reported. In Manasquan, about 34 miles up the coast, roads were also underwater, and Mayor Mike Mangan said he expected "a lot of water in the streets for a long time."

In Sea Bright, Mayor Brian Kelly said he expected this storm to be worse than the one or two floods the borough typically sees each year.

"I think this one will be closer to an Irene-scale flooding event," Kelly told the AP, referring to the 2011 hurricane. "I hope I'm wrong, but that's my gut feeling."

The borough opened its recreation center for residents who evacuate.

Nor'easters are common in the fall, but this one arrived while trees are still full of leaves, National Weather Service meteorologist Matthew Belk told the AP. Leaves catch more wind, which raises the risk of falling limbs, power outages and debris on roads.

The storm's north-northeast winds are also unusual, which state officials in New York said could make wind damage worse, according to Gov. Kathy Hochul's office.

The southern shores of Queens, Nassau County and southwestern Suffolk County could see up to 3.5 feet of floodwater in the most vulnerable spots, Gov. Kathy Hochul's office said Saturday. The Long Island Rail Road's Long Beach branch faces delays and partial suspensions because of flooded tracks, and several Queens bus routes are detouring around flooded streets.

NYC Emergency Management just wrapped a coordination call with the National Weather Service and City agencies. Here's where things stand and what's ahead.

What's happened so far⁰🌧️ About half an inch to an inch of rain has fallen across the city.⁰🌬️ Gusts have reached 45 mph…

— NYC Emergency Management (@nycemergencymgt) September 26, 2026

New York City's heaviest rain is expected to begin around 8 p.m. Saturday and continue into Sunday morning, NYC Emergency Management said after a coordination call with the National Weather Service. Bands of rain could fall at up to an inch an hour, with some neighborhoods getting 2 to 3 inches overnight and isolated flash flooding possible.

Officials called tonight through late Sunday morning the worst time to travel. Gusts of 45 to 55 mph are expected to continue, with an isolated gust near 60 mph possible, bringing more downed trees and outages.

The next high tide arrives around 8:15 to 9 p.m. on the city's south shore and near midnight along Long Island Sound, with moderate flooding expected in Jamaica Bay and the Rockaways. Sunday's midday tide could bring moderate flooding to the coastal Bronx and northern Queens, including parts of Flushing and Astoria, officials said.

Residents can report damage at reportdamage.nyc.gov, and basement apartment residents can gov/notify.

About 84,600 homes and businesses were without power across New Jersey, Connecticut, New York, Massachusetts and Rhode Island as of about 12:20 p.m. Saturday, according to PowerOutage.us.

New Jersey had the most outages, about 30,500, led by Ocean County with more than 8,500. Connecticut had about 24,600, with roughly 6% of customers out in both New London and Litchfield counties. In New York, about 21,700 customers were without power, including nearly 9,500 in Suffolk County on Long Island.

Wind gusts topped 60 mph in parts of Long Island, southeastern Massachusetts and Rhode Island overnight and Saturday morning, according to reports compiled by the National Weather Service's New York and Boston offices.

Nantucket's airport recorded a 64 mph gust, and Farmingdale Airport on Long Island and Martha's Vineyard Airport both recorded gusts of about 60 mph. Weather stations at Eatons Neck and Stony Brook on Long Island's North Shore measured gusts of 65 to 66 mph.

Closer to New York City, JFK Airport recorded a 56 mph gust Friday night, LaGuardia 46 mph and Newark 47 mph. Boston's Logan Airport recorded 51 mph Saturday morning.

title: Detroit Lions place S Thomas Harper on IR, elevate 2 defenders for Week 3
description: The Detroit Lions make three roster moves ahead of their Week 3 game against the New York Jets.
fullText:
The Detroit Lions' injury woes at safety continue to worsen, as they announced Saturday that they placed safety Thomas Harper on injured reserve. Additionally, the Lions announced the elevation of two defensive players for their Week 3 game against the New York Jets, giving the unit more depth for the game.

Harper finished the Lions game against the Bills in Week 2, but suffered an ankle injury that required a walking boot. When practices began on Wednesday, Harper still needed the walking boot for support, but told Detroit News' Rich Silva that he was "just trying to stay off of it" and that it "shouldn't be (a) long-term" injury. Things were apparently more significant than Harper anticipated because he couldn't practice the rest of the week, was ruled out for Week 3 on Friday, and was placed on IR on Saturday. Harper will be required to miss the next four weeks and will not be eligible to return to the roster until Week 7, at the earliest.

Avonte Maddox was also placed on injured reserve this week—his injury will require surgery and is season-ending—and Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph remain on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list, meaning that the Lions are now down four of their top five options at safety.

So what's the plan moving forward?

For Week 3, the Lions will shift Christian Izen from his starting nickel role to a starting safety role, lining up opposite veteran Chuck Clark.

"Izzy's been working a lot back there and had a full week. And he's gotten a ton of work and this week a ton of reps, full-speed reps," Campbell said on Friday. "'This is what you're going to do, these are the calls,' and just dousing him with full-speed reps, and he's done a good job this week. […] Izzy's going to be a huge part for us."

As for their reserve roles, the Lions have three potential options, the most immediate being the game elevation of veteran safety Jalen Mills. Earlier this week, Mills re-signed with the Lions' practice squad to bolster the team's depth at safety. Mills is entering his 11th season in the NFL and spent time on the Lions roster late last season, playing in three games down the stretch. His familiarity with the defensive coverage scheme should help him get up to speed quickly and provide an immediate role against the Jets in Week 3.

The Lions' next option is rookie corner Keith Abney, who was getting "sprinkles back there a little bit as a reserve," according to Campbell. While he's primarily played nickel in Detroit, Abney has the intelligence and ability to work at safety in a pinch.

"For a rookie, he's a pretty dang smart, conscientious, aware football player that's got a ton of room to really take off," Campbell said of Abney on Friday. "So, that's a good sign. […] He just needs reps and reps. But if we need it, that'll be a guy who may have to go in for us."

Lastly, the Lions also poached rookie Bishop Fitzgerald off the Steelers' practice squad earlier in the week, and while he's surely not versed enough in the playbook to get meaningful snaps right now, he'll be an option in their safety depth moving forward. Fitzgerald is an ideal free safety in the Lions scheme because he can ballhawk from center field and be a willing tackler in run support. He'll need time to acclimate, but he has plus developmental upside.

In addition to Mills, the Lions also elevated linebacker Amen Ogbongbemiga from the practice squad for this game. With rookie linebacker Jimmy Rolder slowly returning from a hamstring injury and Joe Bachie recently released from the active roster, Ogbongbemiga will provide the Lions with LB6 depth and a role on multiple phases of special teams.

Impeachment of the Republican president and Cabinet officials is not off the table.

fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda, with investigations of President Donald Trump, his family and his administration if the party sweeps control of the chamber from Republicans in the November elections.

The undertaking is as robust as it is daunting, spanning several House committees. With majority power comes bigger budgets and staff, and the ability to investigate, subpoena and potentially course-correct what the Democrats say are widespread corruption and abuses of power. Impeachment of the Republican president and Cabinet officials is not off the table.

"There is a cost to the American people of the out-of-control corruption," said Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker if Democrats win control at the Capitol.

"If folks have been stealing from the American people, shortchanging the American people or screwing over the American people," Jeffries said, "we are going to hold the crooks accountable."

Congress has enormous ability to conduct oversight of the executive branch as part of its power as a coequal branch of government, and a road map for the Democratic-run investigations has already been set by the almost daily letters lawmakers send to the administration and in amicus court filings.

Democrats are asking about the money-making by Trump and his family, whose wealth has grown dramatically since he returned to the White House in January 2025. They are investigating the potential civil rights violations of Americans killed protesting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations and of detained immigrants being deported to faraway countries. They have fought the closing of the Kennedy Center, launched investigations into private funding of the America at 250 celebrations and tracked the shuttering of federal operations, including the U.S. Agency for International Development.

New questions emerge daily, including the Trump family's recent acknowledgment that a weekend wedding party for the president's son Donald Trump Jr. was partly funded by a Russian oligarch, with reportedly close ties to the Kremlin.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is in line to become the chairman of the Judiciary Committee, characterized the issues involved as "gargantuan."

"We need to zero in quickly on the forms of systemic corruption that have cost the public huge amounts of money," Raskin told The Associated Press, "and where there are legislative cures available."

Jeffries will almost certainly be under pressure from the far left to move more swiftly to articles of impeachment against Trump, who during his first became the first president to be twice impeached by the House. Both times, he was acquitted by the Senate.

Impeaching the president a third time may not hold the currency that it once did. Democrats will more likely focus their impeachment efforts on Cabinet members. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth already faces articles of impeachment from a Republican, Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, over his leadership at the Pentagon and his management of the Iran war.

"We haven't ruled anything out," Jeffries said recently about the tools available to Congress, "and we haven't ruled anything in."

The White House is likely to play hardball if confronted with investigations, and Democrats are bracing for an administration that potentially ignores subpoenas or refuses to turn over paperwork that lawmakers are demanding.

The Democrats are also reaching beyond the administration into various corporate and business entities for potential wrongdoing.

Ranking Democratic lawmakers who are in line to lead committees if power shifts are beginning to chart the investigations they plan to tackle.

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat now on the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has outlined five priorities, including Trump family business dealings, the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and ICE operations.

"We're already doing work," Garcia told the AP.

He also mentioned the Department of Health and Human Services under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as well as broader allegations of corporate corruption.

The top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, whose jurisdiction includes the State Department, said the committee plans to investigate Trump's international dealings, including around the Iran war.

He expects the committee will also look into the administration's Venezuela operations — from the military strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific waters to the U.S. partnership with a private company to develop and access the South American country's oil.

Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the ranking Democrat at the Natural Resources Committee, which overseas the Interior Department and its National Park Service operations, has begun digging into Trump's "vanity projects," including the demolition of the White House's East wing for a new ballroom and the president's proposed arch.

Huffman and other committee members have also been eyeing the Trump family's role in various minerals deals.

At the committee's last session before lawmakers recessed to campaign for the midterm elections, Huffman said that if Democrats take charge, he plans to call witnesses, put them under oath and follow the evidence where it leads.

"When people ask what will we do," he said he responds, "My answer is simple. We'll use those tools. We'll act like the Congress."

fullText:
Millions of people along the East Coast are bracing for a powerful nor'easter that is expected to bring heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding from the Carolinas to Maine, forecasters say.

The storm, which formed off the mid-Atlantic coast, is expected to stall as it approaches the Northeast and New England, according to the National Weather Service, increasing the likelihood of flooding and beach erosion in parts of New Jersey, New York, Connecticut, Rhode Island and Massachusetts.

The Jersey Shore, Long Island and Cape Cod could see up to 3 feet of inundation, especially during high tides.

"This storm may be remembered for its destructive coastal flooding and severe beach erosion, especially along eastern Long Island and the Massachusetts coast," AccuWeather Chief Meteorologist Jon Porter said.

The system has already caused coastal flooding in parts of North Carolina, Virginia, Maryland and Delaware. A stretch of highway on North Carolina's Outer Banks was closed due to "severe overwash" on the roadway.

"We expect similar conditions to continue over the next few high tide cycles until the storm passes," North Carolina's Department of Transportation said on Facebook. "There is currently no timeline on reopening the highway."

Curious what's coming next where you live? Check the new Yahoo Weather app.

Wind gusts of up to 55 mph are expected across the region, which could lead to widespread power outages.

"Given long-duration wind and rain under full foliage, damaging winds will blow down numerous tree limbs, scattered trees and power lines," the National Weather Service's New York office warned.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani issued a travel advisory, encouraging residents to allow extra time and avoid low-lying coastal roads during high tide.

"If you live in a basement apartment, know your way out and be prepared to move to a higher floor if conditions become dangerous," the mayor said in a post on X.

Up to 5 inches of rain is possible in some areas, including eastern Long Island, Rhode Island and Massachusetts.

In anticipation of travel delays, three major airlines — American, United and JetBlue — waived fees for flight changes for travelers from New York City to Boston Friday through Sunday.

The storm has already prompted the organizers of Oceans Calling in Ocean City, Md., to cancel the three-day music festival.

"Tides, floods, and high winds have prevented us from safely continuing the build of Oceans Calling," the festival said in a statement. "Following the advice of the National Weather Service and in cooperation with local public officials, we must make the difficult decision to cancel Oceans Calling 2026."

The Global Citizen Festival, scheduled for Saturday in Central Park, was also canceled.

All Things Go NYC, a three-day music festival set for Forest Hills Stadium in Queens, N.Y., was scrapped by its organizers. But All Things Go D.C., at Merriweather Post Pavilion in Columbia, Md., remains scheduled for this weekend.

The New York Yankees moved Saturday's home game against the Baltimore Orioles up a day due to the impending nor'easter. The clubs are now scheduled to play a single-admission doubleheader on Friday. The Boston Red Sox moved Sunday's home game against the Chicago Cubs to Friday, when the teams will play a doubleheader.

Ed Sheeran's controversial tour canceled two shows that had been scheduled for Gillette Stadium in Foxboro, Mass., due to the forecast.

"Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium," the tour's promoter, Messina Touring, said in a statement posted to Instagram. "The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority."

fullText:
CAIRO/DUBAI Sept 25 (Reuters) - Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani military chiefs are to discuss help for Saudi Arabia as it faces attacks by Yemen's Houthis, while Iraq further curtailed Iranian flights on Friday, in line with US pressure, and an Iranian official threatened retaliation.

The Houthis have launched strikes on the Saudi-backed government ‌in Yemen and repeatedly fired into Saudi Arabia, disrupting oil flows from the world's largest energy exporter, as part of a wider Middle East war that began with US and ‌Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.

The military escalation continued this week despite a push during the UN General Assembly in New York to revive diplomacy to end the conflict, which quickly spread to Lebanon and the Gulf in March before escalating ​in Yemen in recent weeks.

With talks stalled and during a lull in direct fire by the US and Iran, Washington had shifted tactics to extend financial sanctions by targeting companies from third countries that do business with Iranian firms through "secondary sanctions".

Iranian airlines were barred from neighbouring countries including the United Arab Emirates and Oman on Thursday in response to new US sanctions, the first big impact of the shift.

On Friday, the three other Iraqi airports that operate flights to and from Iran joined Baghdad airport in suspending them, sources and state media said.

A flight ban, if sustained, could deepen Iran's isolation and worsen an economic crisis in the ‌country, which is already facing a US blockade of its seaports.

Mohammad Mokhber, ⁠an adviser to Iran's supreme leader, accused regional countries of "alignment with America" for blocking flights.

"If Iran does not have the possibility to fly and receive airport services, then no country in the region will have this possibility either", he said in a social media post.

The war, which US President Donald Trump ⁠launched alongside Israel, has killed thousands of people and disrupted global trade and energy supplies, adding to inflationary pressures.

While the fighting between the US and Iran has been stop-start, Iranian allies have mobilised, with Hezbollah attacks triggering an Israeli invasion of Lebanon and the Houthi advance in Yemen prompting a new humanitarian crisis.

Iran and its allies have significantly squeezed oil exports from Saudi Arabia, a US ally. The Houthis have disrupted ship traffic at the mouth ​of ​the Red Sea, while Iran has limited tanker traffic at the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for 20% of ​the world's oil exports before the war.

On Thursday, the Houthis said they had ‌fired dozens of missiles and drones at Saudi targets, while Saudi authorities said they had intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Houthi fighters.

Later, Saudi Arabia's Grand Mufti, the kingdom's top religious authority, called on soldiers to be ready to lay down their lives to fight the Houthis until the group was ousted from power.

Amid the fighting, the Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish foreign ministers met on Thursday for discussions under a defence pact signed in August.

They condemned attacks targeting the holy Saudi city of Mecca and other civilian sites, while affirming Saudi Arabia's right to defend itself and planning a meeting between chiefs of staff on ways to assist the kingdom.

Turkey's defence ministry said Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu was travelling to Saudi Arabia on Friday to meet his Saudi and Pakistani counterparts.

Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said the defence pact, which ‌stipulates that an attack against one country be considered an attack against all, could lead to intelligence, logistical or ​ammunition support.

"More advanced military support could also be considered depending on the scale of the threat," Erdogan said in written ​responses to Newsweek.

The speaker of Turkey's parliament, which has yet to ratify the pact, said ​it could be expanded into a broader alliance "for the Muslim world", including Iran.

In New York, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told reporters on ‌Thursday that Tehran had conveyed a proposal to the US via intermediaries ​under which the Strait of Hormuz would be reopened ​if Tehran's conditions were met.

Under Iran's proposal, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon, within seven days. The US would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran's frozen funds and waive its oil sanctions, he said.

"The Strait of Hormuz will be reopened on the last day," Araqchi said, adding that talks with the US on other issues, including Iran's nuclear issue, ​would then start.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday that Tehran was ‌reviewing Washington's response to its peace proposals.

Oil prices fell on Friday as markets weighed the possibility of a truce, despite the number of ships recorded transiting the Strait of ​Hormuz dropping to nine on Thursday, half the 10-day average.

title: Iran's president says Tehran wants a deal with U.S. before the midterms
description:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addressing the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Wednesday. (Selcuk Acar / Anadolu via Getty Images)
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday suggested his government was willing to make a deal with the U.S.
fullText:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday suggested his government was willing to make a deal with the U.S. to end the war before Americans head to the polls this November.

“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Pezeshkian said in a brief meeting with NBC News and other news organizations on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

“We wish Americans to return to the MOU before the midterms,” Pezeshkian added, referring to a memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Iran that laid out plans for a temporary ceasefire. The agreement, signed in June, eventually collapsed.

In response to NBC News’ request for comment, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said: “The Iranian regime has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region.”

“The President is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable,” Kelly added.

Pezeshkian’s comments came two days after President Donald Trump said in a speech to world leaders at the U.N. that he believed the Iranian regime would not make a deal to settle the conflict until after the fall elections.

“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”

Polls show Democrats with an advantage heading into the November contests. The latest NBC News Decision Desk Poll found 31% of respondents approved of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, while 69% disapproved.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told a group of reporters in a separate briefing in New York on Thursday that a plan has been presented to U.S. officials through mediators during talks this week that would lead to the opening of the Strait of Hormuz and the resumption of talks after seven days.

Araghchi said the plan could begin as soon as the U.S. agreed to it and maintained that the plan did not go beyond the agreement signed by Trump in June, commonly referred to as a memorandum of understanding.

“We have introduced a plan to the United States through the intermediators that, if certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will be open at the end of seven days and talks will be restarted,” Araghchi said. “The conditions we have asked the U.S. to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the U.S. president.”

Araghchi pointed out that one of the conditions of the plan is for the U.S. to accept a maritime transit route through the Strait of Hormuz that has been agreed upon by Iran and Oman.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump on Tuesday also defended the conflict and said he was considering whether to “annihilate” the country or make a deal.

Trump has repeatedly said that the goal of attacking Iran was to prevent the development of a nuclear weapon. Soon after the war started, Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the conflict, sending shock waves through the world economy.

In the exchange with news organizations, Pezeshkian said he has met with the Islamic Republic’s new leader twice — including a month ago, for seven hours.

Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei assumed the role in early March after his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in an Israeli attack that also killed family members and other senior leaders.

Pezeshkian said he did not see “any issues with his health or physical appearance” in their meetings, adding that they sat on the floor on traditional pillows. Mojtaba Khamenei was severely injured in the strike that killed his father, three people with knowledge of the matter told NBC News in July, with burns to his face and body and wounds that have required several operations to one of his legs.

Iran’s president briefly addressed other pressing issues affecting the relationship between Tehran and Washington. He said his government was “open” to inspections of its nuclear facilities, which the regime has long maintained are for civilian purposes, and he insisted the regime was not seeking to assassinate the American president.

“This has not been the position of the Iranian government that we seek to assassinate President Trump or his family members,” Pezeshkian said.

The Justice Department charged an Iranian man in November in an alleged murder-for-hire effort to kill Trump when he was the Republican presidential candidate in 2024.

Two others were charged with planning to kill an Iranian American journalist and activist who has criticized the Iranian government over its treatment of women.

U.S. authorities said the plot was part of Iran’s efforts to avenge the death of a top Iranian general, Qassem Soleimani, who was killed in Baghdad in a U.S. drone strike Trump ordered during his first term in the White House.

Pezeshkian has previously denied an Iranian plot to kill Trump, telling NBC News’ Lester Holt in Tehran last year that the regime would “never” do so.

fullText:
The New York Knicks are preparing to defend their first NBA championship in 53 years, but a key player faces an uncertain future. Karl-Anthony Towns helped New York beat the San Antonio Spurs in the Finals, but his contract situation remains unsettled before training camp.

Towns is eligible for a four-year extension worth up to $276 million. ESPN's Shams Charania reported that talks have stalled and that an agreement is unlikely before training camp begins.

The Knicks and Towns discussed an extension for much of the offseason, but little progress has been made recently. Talks could continue during the season, although ESPN reported that a deal is not expected soon.

The timing adds pressure to the situation. Towns is entering the final guaranteed year of his contract and will earn $57 million this season. He also has a $61 million player option for the 2027-28 season.

New York has also set a clear financial limit. Owner James Dolan has repeatedly said the Knicks want to avoid the NBA's second apron, which restricts how expensive teams can build and change their rosters. That approach has already come at a cost, as backup center Mitchell Robinson left for the Boston Celtics during the offseason.

Towns enters the contract talks after a strong postseason. He averaged 15.9 points, 10.6 rebounds and 4.9 assists while shooting 55 percent during the playoffs. That production helped New York finish 16-3 and win the championship.

His playoff performance gives him a strong case for a major extension. However, the Knicks also face other costly contract decisions. Josh Hart is eligible for an extension, while Jalen Brunson and OG Anunoby could become eligible next offseason.

New York must now balance two goals. The Knicks want to keep their championship team together, but they also want to avoid pushing the payroll beyond the limit they have set.

Towns remains under contract with the Knicks for the coming season. The main question is whether New York can find a number that keeps its championship core together without crossing its financial line.

title: Giants' John Harbaugh and Matt Nagy will 'build the offense around' Jameis Winston
description: Following the serious knee injury to QB Jaxson Dart, New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh and offensive coordinator Matt Nagy are shifting gears to run the offense around Jameis Winston.
fullText:
Following the potentially season-ending knee injury to quarterback Jaxson Dart, Giants head coach John Harbaugh and offensive coordinator Matt Nagy are shifting gears to run the offense around backup signal-caller Jameis Winston (at least for now).

Winston, aged 32, has plenty of experience as a starting quarterback, most of which came during his time with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the franchise which selected him with the 1st overall pick in the 2015 NFL Draft.

Across 89 starts (including two with the Giants in 2025), Winston has completed 61.1 percent of his passes, averaging 270.0 passing yards and 2.4 sacks per game. In those starts, he's also thrown 150 touchdown passes and 107 interceptions.

"He's a big, strong, passing quarterback who can throw the ball," Harbaugh said of Winston. "His strengths are evident, so that's what you build the offense around."

Nagy agreed with Harbaugh's assessment of the veteran quarterback, comparing and contrasting his skillset with what Dart has shown in his young career thus far.

"Obviously, Dart is a dual threat quarterback" said Nagy. "When you lose that, it impacts the playbook."

"But at the same time, Jameis is a guy who has played a lot of football games in his career. We have ultimate trust in him. Our job as coaches is to help [Jameis] help us, designing the offense around his strengths and what he can do."

Winston has a well-earned reputation for committing turnovers, which was evident in New York's loss against the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night, when he forced a throw in the red zone which was intercepted.

"I have to execute better and I am going to execute better," Winston remarked in the wake of that game.

Nagy acknowledged and addressed Winston's style of play, and explained what he'd like to see out of the makeshift starter moving forward.

"We know who he is. There is a lot of feast or famine with him," Nagy stated. "We talked all training camp about protecting and respecting that football. Ball security is paramount with the type of team that we have."

"Jameis knows that, and he's as true as a pro as you'll see, preparation-wise. Thankfully, he's been here for all the OTA's and training camp, so he'll be prepared."

Harbaugh echoed Nagy's praise of Winston's hard work behind the scenes, and believes it sets him up to be as comfortable as a backup quarterback can reasonably be stepping into the driver's seat.

"All these plays that we have, we've been practicing and running them with [Winston during practice], so it's more like a lane change as opposed to changing direction," the head coach declared.

Winston himself is equal parts thrilled and thankful at the opportunity to prove that he is as a starting-caliber quarterback in the NFL with the Giants.

"This is what I've always dreamed of, to be a starting quarterback," Winston stated. "Obviously, my respects and gratitude are just going to be with Jaxson, but at the same time, this is what I dream of, being where I am right now and executing at a high level."

"Execution and preparation are the same," he continued. "Football is my priority, so every single day I write down what I would love, and that's to be a Super Bowl winning, starting NFL quarterback, so my schedule is always planned around executing that."

Winston is no stranger to season-derailing injuries. In fact, in Week 8 of the 2021 season, while playing for the New Orleans Saints, Winston suffered a season-ending torn ACL and Grade 2 MCL sprain in his left knee.

It's no surprise, then, that Winston is being vocal about supporting Dart throughout his injury recovery process.

"Me and Jaxson have talked." he explained. "It's pretty fresh, so I'm going to keep on lifting him up. He's a warrior. He's in good spirits. He's focusing on what he would love, and that's healing. And all of us are going to just wrap our arms around him and lift him up."

Finally, Winston spoke on the Giants fanbase regarding their expectations for the team moving forward.

"The fans want to see wins," Winston concluded. "It's not about what I'm showing them, it's about us going out there and winning football games together, giving them something to cheer for, giving them something to stand behind."

The Giants (1-1) host the Titans (0-2) on Sunday at 1 p.m. in a showdown with former head coach Brian Daboll, who now serves as Tennessee's offensive coordinator.

title: Mamdani is the most popular elected official in NYC: poll
description: Nine months into his mayoralty, Mayor Mamdani’s honeymoon phase is still going strong, according to a poll released Wednesday.
fullText:
Nine months into his mayoralty, Mayor Mamdani’s honeymoon phase is still going strong, according to a poll released Wednesday.

Mamdani is the most popular elected official in New York City, a new poll from Quinnipiac found, with his statewide popularity on par with that of Gov. Hochul.

Statewide, 46% of likely voters said they have a favorable opinion of Mamdani, while 36% had an unfavorable opinion of him and 15% haven’t heard enough about him. The Quinnipiac poll came out the same day as a similar Siena poll, which found he had the same favorable rating but a 44% unfavorable rating.

The poll found that, when broken by gender, Mamdani did ten points better among women statewide.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez received a 41% favorable and 36% unfavorable rating across the state; Sen. Chuck Schumer got 34% to 51% unfavorable, and the Democratic Socialists of America, the organization that has shaped much of both Mamdani and AOC’s political identity, received a rating of 29% favorable to 43% unfavorable.

Gov. Hochul received a 46%-43% favorability rating statewide, with her numbers growing to 53% favorable among likely voters from New York City.

The poll, which surveyed 1,026 likely voters across the state with a margin of error of +/- 4.1 percentage points, showed Hochul with a comfortable lead over Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman, with 58% of likely voters supporting Hochul and 39% supporting Blakeman.

Among likely voters in the five boroughs, Mamdani nets a whopping 60% favorability rating, with 29% saying they don’t have a favorable opinion of him.

That’s higher than the local favorability ratings of not just Hochul, but also AOC and Schumer, who received 50%-30% favorability ratings and 32%-55%, respectively. AOC has not ruled out a 2028 run for either Schumer’s Senate seat or the presidency.

“As Democrats try to regain control of Congress, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s scores are underwater in his home state. It’s worth noting Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is seen in a more positive light at a time when she’s being closely watched as she decides her political future and whether it might include a challenge to Schumer,” Quinnipiac University Poll Assistant Director Mary Snow said in a statement.

These numbers come as the midterms loom, although Mamdani has not committed to using his influence to weigh in on races outside New York, telling CNN this week he was more focused on filling potholes than getting involved in national politics. AOC, for her part, has donated $300,000 to New York State Democrats and is slated to campaign for Democrats in upstate New York this week.

Mamdani endorsed Hochul back in February. The governor has said she expects help from Mamdani in her reelection bid.

fullText:
Sept 24 (Reuters) - US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, sources close to the talks said.

The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the ‌global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.

The talks face a big obstacle as neither side wants to be the first to surrender its leverage, according to comments to Reuters by two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomatic sources, but behind Iran's ‌stance is a recognition of the economic cost of prolonged confrontation.

A senior Iranian official said the most plausible way to end the impasse would be a phased arrangement, with Iran allowing navigation through Hormuz in return for the US lifting its economic blockade and Tehran potentially gaining access to frozen assets.

"One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would ​be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz," he said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

That would involve US President Donald Trump accepting another temporary fix, after an earlier understanding collapsed in July. So a central challenge facing the negotiators is not just to sketch out a deal but also to ensure any concessions are durable enough for both sides to trust, the sources said.

Trump has said he thinks the US and Iran could reach a deal after midterm elections to Congress on November 3. A senior European official said the Iranians "have a very long list of demands."

A White House official said that while "Iran is desperate for a deal, President Trump holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States."

Trump, he said, remained "open to talking with Iran under the right circumstances" but had no need to negotiate, and the US was in a "very strong position" with control of the Strait of Hormuz and an Iranian economy that ‌was "collapsing."

The official said "crushing sanctions" and "one of the most successful blockades in history" have crippled Iran's economy and left ⁠Iran completely broke. Trump was content to let the "inevitable Iranian collapse" play out rather than be "played" by Tehran, the official said.

Former US negotiator Dennis Ross said he saw only a 30% chance of an agreement being reached before the vote, but that both sides may have stronger reasons to make a deal before than after the midterms.

"The blockade is what's really squeezing the Iranians. It's strangling them," Ross said.

A deal before the midterms could benefit Trump, as reopening Hormuz could ⁠ease tensions in the Gulf, contain oil prices and help bring down politically sensitive US gasoline prices.

Iran's chances of gaining much-needed economic relief may be greater while Trump still has a greater political incentive to strike a bargain.

After the midterms, Ross said, Trump may face fewer constraints and be more willing to intensify pressure or consider military options.

The leverage that brought Washington and Tehran back to negotiations could also make compromise harder.

Washington controls the pressure that is hurting Tehran most, while Tehran controls access to a critical energy chokepoint. Neither side wants to surrender that leverage without extracting something tangible in return.

This means the midterms may be less a deadline for diplomacy than ​for ​preserving the conditions that make the diplomatic efforts possible. If Washington and Tehran cannot turn leverage into a deal before the midterms, the diplomatic window could narrow as the ​risk of escalation grows.

Even as it seeks a diplomatic off-ramp, Tehran is preparing for the possibility of renewed war with ‌Washington, the Iranian official said, accusing the US of using the economic blockade and threat of force as tools of coercion.

"Our fingers are on the trigger," said the senior Iranian official. "The Americans know what they need to do but, because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this are extremely low."

Regional sources said Tehran was willing to drop a demand for payment of transit fees to use the Strait of Hormuz from the main agreement and put the demand in a side attachment instead, as ending the blockade had become the more urgent priority.

Gulf states have rejected the proposal for payment of transit fees. Any arrangement would be temporary, not a formal abandonment of Iran's position, the regional sources said.

The US has tightened the economic vice on Iran, layering new sanctions on top of a blockade that has choked off Iran's oil exports, an important source of hard currency.

This month, it targeted Iran's remaining commercial airlines and support networks as part of a campaign to sever the economic lifelines sustaining the government and the powerful Revolutionary Guards. Trump warned that Iran's economy could "rot" unless it reached a deal.

"Iran is not primarily focused on imposing tolls in Hormuz but on preserving its administrative control of the waterway," he ‌said. "Iran may be willing to defer the toll issue, but they are not going to give up administrative control of the strait."

At the heart of the diplomacy in New ​York is a fundamental tension. Washington wants pressure to produce concessions, Tehran wants pressure removed before making them, and the Gulf states want the conflict resolved without allowing the region's strategic waterways ​to become enduring bargaining chips.

FEARS OF AN OPEN-ENDED CONFLICT

During a separate meeting with Trump in New York, Gulf leaders sought clarity on Washington's ​endgame beyond the midterms, including on whether the US would resume military action if Iran refused to return to negotiations.

They conveyed their collective rejection of any Iranian control of Hormuz, saying freedom of navigation must be restored and that the strategic ‌waterway should not become a tool of coercion against Gulf states, regional sources said.

Yet alongside their warnings over ​Hormuz, Gulf leaders have pressed hard for de-escalation and a political process, reflecting the ​region's determination to stay out of any further conflict between the US and Iran.

"It's still not clear what Trump's endgame is, or what the alternative to the pressure campaign would be," said Ebtessam al-Ketbi, president of the Emirates Policy Center think tank based in Abu Dhabi.

"The Iranians, by contrast, know what they want. They're reshaping the regional landscape through Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb with a clear objective while Washington has yet to define its roadmap," she said, referring to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

That ​uncertainty is also shaping Tehran's calculations. Danny Citrinowicz, a regional analyst and former Israeli military intelligence officer, said the ‌New York talks had not altered the basic positions of either side and that Iran was unlikely to retreat as long as it believed Trump wanted to avoid a wider escalation before the midterms.

"The blockade is hurting them, but rather than softening their ​position, it is likely to drive them to escalate because they believe that if they soften their position, they are dead," said Alan Eyre, a former US negotiator on Iran.

A Western official familiar with the talks added: "It is all about opening the Strait ​of Hormuz. We're all under pressure domestically and the Iranians know that."

fullText:
Activists gathered outside the OpenAI offices on Monday during climate week in New York City

On Monday evening, protesters gathered outside the unmarked Manhattan offices of OpenAI, maker of ChatGPT, holding signs calling to “Eat the rich, save the planet”. Over the next two days, groups also picketed outside the offices of fellow tech giants Google and Amazon; other protesters, including clergy, were arrested while disrupting a closed-door AI health summit in the city. Tonight, protesters will target a Brooklyn gas power plant that was set to close – until it was purchased to power AI datacenters.

The protests come on the heels of an Anthropic employee quitting his job with a warning that intensified an already-growing AI panic: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Though it was far from the first time an AI expert had issued a doomsday message about the threat the tech poses, this time it dominated public attention, arriving as trust in big tech has hit an all-time low and communities across the country are trying to stop the building of datacenters. From 2024 to 2026, at least $64bn in proposed datacenter buildout was blocked by local organizing. Today, bans have been passed in at least 18 states at the local or county level, and New York passed a statewide moratorium this summer.

“They are claiming that they have the power to end humanity, but at the same time can’t get AI to do a lot of major things that they’re pushing for,” said Jonathan Westin of Climate Defenders and the Stop Funding Billionaires campaign, which organized the “unplug AI” week of action.

Like Westin, many of the protesters at the anti-AI protests this week were part of climate organizations, in town for New York’s climate week, a global gathering of elected officials, policy experts and advocates timed to the meeting of the United Nations general assembly. Datacenters require significant amounts of water to function and an immense amount of energy to power, often using fossil fuels, bringing pollution into communities. Organizers are calling for more datacenter moratoriums and stronger commitments to protect water access and to block fossil fuels. They say tech companies’ greed is the real threat to the environment.

Even Wall Street has warned the AI boom could cause another economic bubble to burst – one that, protesters say, will be carried on the backs of working Americans. “Regular people shouldn’t be left holding the bag for a bunch of billionaires and trillionaires to play Monopoly with our economy,” Westin said.

Other groups at this week’s protests, like the anti-war organization Code Pink, called attention to how many big tech corporations work with the US military: the US has used tech made by Palantir, xAI and Anthropic to establish targets and rain down bombs in the war in Iran – all with far-from-perfect accuracy.

Alex Hanna, director of research at the Dair Institute, an AI research organization centering communities facing environmental damage and extraction from AI, said the doomsday prophesying from tech companies and former employees are a distraction amid “the climate and ecological crisis, the rising fascism that is borne out of climate politics, the making of climate refugees, and the growing inability of people just to get by from day to day. It’s such a disconnect from what seems to be actually happening.”

Some protesters outside the OpenAI offices Monday had traveled from New Mexico, where a planned datacenter threatens the already-sapped Rio Grande and a community facing a 20-year drought. Oracle’s Project Jupiter, which is contracted to OpenAI, was pitched as a job creator for the community, but organizers say the companies aren’t talking about how it would drain the area’s limited water resources.

“There’s just so much misinformation that’s being sold, not only to the elected [officials], but to the community, and I think it’s really a disservice to the people of New Mexico for these companies to come in and just basically lie about what they’re going to do and how these projects are going to benefit communities,” said Daisy Maldonado, a resident of Doña Ana county, the planned site of the datacenter.

At an AI sustainability conference elsewhere in the city on Tuesday, five protesters were arrested for disrupting a keynote on using AI to solve the energy grid crisis. Activists called out the conference framing as “greenwashing”, or using misleading descriptions to brand something as eco-friendly or less harmful. “We do not want to greenwash these datacenters that are being built,” said Adrosto de Silva, who also traveled from New Mexico to the OpenAI protest. “There is no way that you can do harm reduction in any sort of datacenter whatsoever.”

At Monday’s protest, attendees – including the Tennessee state representative Justin Jones, who dropped in while in town for climate week – emphasized that many of these fights are happening in communities of color and poor communities, where the companies thought they wouldn’t face local backlash.

“This building behind me is a danger to humankind,” said Jones, gesturing at the OpenAI offices. “The confluence of this techno oligarchy is a threat to us all. I’m here because if they come for one of us, they’re coming for all of us.”

fullText:
Sunny Hostin told her fellow panelists on “The View” that she was the holdout juror responsible for “The Butcher of Tompkins Square Park” being found not guilty by reason of insanity in his 1991 murder trial.

East Village resident Daniel Rakowitz was charged with killing and mutilating a female acquaintance in 1989, then trying to get rid of the evidence by making soup out of her remains and serving it in Tompkins Square Park.

Hostin said on Tuesday that she felt a connection to the murder trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy, whose case ended in a Sept. 4 mistrial with all but one juror believing the defendant’s compromises mental state exempted her from criminal culpability.

“The reason … I feel so strongly about this holdout juror is because I was a holdout juror in a case, in the Daniel Rakowitz case,” she said to her shocked castmates.

Hostin, whose name was Asuncion Cummings at the time, said she sat on the jury before starting law school. She went on to become a federal prosecutor, then a television legal analyst.

To make her point, Hostin read a New York Times article about the case that mentions her resistance.

“Several jurors questioned afterwards said one holdout juror was principally responsible for preventing them from returning a guilty verdict,” the article said.

She continued telling her story to her stunned colleagues.

“That was me, and it was because clearly I saw he was psychotic, he was in psychosis, he did not mean to kill her and once he killed her he panicked.  the 57-year-old legal expert explained. “He chopped up her body parts, yes, boiled her body parts, tried to commit the perfect crime.”

Hostin said one angry juror threw a chair at her, but she wouldn’t budge. Eventually the other jurors saw things her way.

“The insanity defense is a real thing,” she said.

She defended her position Monday by saying Rakowitz remains incarcerated in the Kirby Forensic Psychiatric Center on Ward’s Island where he’s receiving treatment and poses no threat to the public.

Massachusetts prosecutors haven’t announced whether they intend to try Clancy again in a criminal court. Her defense team argues the 36-year-old suspect was suffering from postpartum psychosis when she killer her three young children in their suburban Boston home. She’s currently being held in a state-run psychiatric hospital.

fullText:
TEL AVIV, Sept 24 (Reuters) - Benjamin Netanyahu is expected to use his UN address on Thursday to berate New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani for calling him a war criminal, a feud that highlights the Israeli leader's growing isolation ahead of elections at home that he may lose.

Addressing the mayor directly ‌in a video statement this week, Netanyahu said he was going to New York "to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers" and "to tell the truth about you." He falsely accused ‌Mamdani of supporting Hamas militants.

Mamdani campaigned for office on a promise to have Netanyahu arrested for alleged war crimes should he visit the largest US city but later said he determined he lacked the legal authority to do so. This ​week, Mamdani described Netanyahu as "the architect of a horrific genocide against Palestinians."

Netanyahu, who rejects war crimes allegations, will be making his first visit to New York since Mamdani took office in January. Israelis opposed to Netanyahu's right-wing government are planning to protest in New York.

Ahead of his speech, Netanyahu's government paid to place 500 pro-Israel and anti-Iran billboards and dozens of trucks carrying messages in support of Israel across Manhattan, Netanyahu's office said in a statement.

"Freedom doesn't defend itself. America and Israel stand together against terror," one of the billboards states. Under it appears the subtext: "Paid for by the State of Israel".

NETANYAHU ADDRESS TO RESEMBLE 'CAMPAIGN SPEECH'

Israel ‌holds a general election in five weeks that opinion polls suggest could ⁠end Netanyahu's long hold on power.

The campaign is unfolding amid mounting criticism of Israel's Gaza war and without a planned meeting with US President Donald Trump.

"He's not really speaking to the UN, he's speaking to the Israeli public," said former Israeli Ambassador Michael Oren, who expects Netanyahu's address to resemble a "campaign speech."

"Maybe ⁠he's thinking, 'If I can attack Mamdani and attack the Iranians, somebody who was wavering between voting for me and voting for (Gadi) Eisenkot may decide to vote for me,'" Oren said, referring to former military chief Eisenkot, Netanyahu's leading rival.

NETANYAHU NOT EXPECTED TO MEET TRUMP

Netanyahu is making an unusually short visit to the US for his UN address. He arrived in New York around 9 a.m. ET (1300 GMT) and is expected to fly back the ​same ​day after delivering his speech in the afternoon.

The Israeli leader is to meet with the presidents of Argentina, ​Bolivia, Ethiopia, Panama and Paraguay and the vice president of Colombia, and with the ‌prime ministers of Greece, Papua New Guinea and Slovenia, Netanyahu's office said. His office did not say if meetings were planned with US officials.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, two Israeli officials earlier said Netanyahu's team was discussing potentially holding meetings with senior US officials including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, though nothing had been set.

Netanyahu is not expected to meet Trump. The two men jointly launched a war on Iran on February 28, but they found themselves on a collision course after the US and Iran agreed to an interim ceasefire that Netanyahu opposed.

Many Israelis were angered by that deal, and opinion polls showed they questioned Trump's commitment to Israeli security, even as his administration proceeds with billions of dollars in arms sales to Israel's government.

"A lack of any encounter with the president, a month ‌before an Israeli election, will indicate that Trump is keeping a distance from him and will be negative for ​Netanyahu's campaign," said Nimrod Goren, president of Mitvim, an Israeli think tank focused on the country's foreign policy.

The election ​is scheduled for October 27.

ISRAEL CONFRONTS INTERNATIONAL CRITICISM

Israel's longest-serving prime minister, Netanyahu has in the ​past made a visual spectacle of his UN appearances, using charts, diagrams and props to warn of Iran's nuclear program, which Tehran says is for civilian ‌purposes.

Last year several delegations walked out as Netanyahu approached the lectern while supporters ​in the gallery cheered.

Goren said Netanyahu's speech would likely ​follow a familiar script: defending Israel, confronting its critics and warning about Iran while arguing that Israel's opposition to Tehran serves the interests of the wider international community.

He will also likely tout what he sees as his own achievements and close ties to Trump and the US, Goren said.

Israel has faced deepening diplomatic isolation since launching its war in Gaza in ​response to the Hamas-led attacks on Israel nearly three years ago.

Netanyahu ‌is unable to travel to many countries because of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant, issued against him and his former defense minister as well as the then-military commander ​of Hamas in 2024.

Earlier this month, once-steadfast allies Britain, France and Canada announced sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which drew a muted response from ​Washington.

fullText:
The full fury of a significant September nor'easter will target New England, where high winds lead to power outages and heavy rain swamps outdoor activities this weekend.

The storm and its effects are occurring through the full moon this weekend, which will raise tide levels and lead to major coastal flooding. Long-duration pounding surf will cause extensive beach erosion from North Carolina to southern Maine.

"This storm may be remembered for its destructive coastal flooding and severe beach erosion, especially along eastern Long Island and the Massachusetts coast," AccuWeather Chief Meteorologist Jon Porter said.

Storm surge, tidal flooding into Friday

The pressure difference between high pressure over the interior Northeast and developing low pressure off the mid-Atlantic coast is strengthening northeast winds from North Carolina to New York. These winds are pushing ocean and bay waters toward shore, causing coastal flooding. Flooding will be worst around high tide through Friday in the mid-Atlantic region.

Water levels will be 2-3 feet above the average monthly tide level, with some locations approaching 6 feet above that level. The worst conditions are forecast for southeastern Virginia, where water will become trapped at the lower end of the Chesapeake Bay, causing backups along the region's tidal rivers. Areas in Virginia Beach, Norfolk and Newport News, Virginia, will be inundated for hours at a time.

Farther north from the Delmarva Peninsula to northern New Jersey, tides will be 1-2 feet above the monthly average, with some areas near 3 feet above.

Storm to strengthen, hook into New England this weekend

The nor'easter will affect southeastern New England from Friday into Sunday. The strongest winds and heaviest rain are expected from Friday night through Saturday night across Rhode Island, central and eastern Massachusetts, eastern Connecticut, southeastern New Hampshire and the southern Maine coast.

Damaging winds will pose the greatest threat across southeastern New England, with gusts potentially reaching hurricane force and causing tree damage and power outages.

"Many trees still have their leaves, which catch more wind and place additional strain on their roots, further increasing the risk for trees to come down and may also increase the number of power outages as compared to similar storms," Porter said.

Rain last week left the soil soggy, increasing the risk that strong winds will uproot trees, AccuWeather Senior Meteorologist Joe Lundberg said.

Falling trees could damage power lines and cause widespread outages.

As the storm approaches New England, strengthening east-northeast winds will push Atlantic water toward shore. Water will pile up in Cape Cod Bay and other bays, sounds, harbors and inlets from Long Island to Maine, flooding low-lying coastal areas.

The storm will draw moisture northward from the subtropical Atlantic, fueling heavy rain across southeastern New England.

Periods of heavy rain across southeastern New England through the weekend could flood streets and small streams, disrupt travel and force changes to outdoor plans.

Rainfall will generally total 1-2 inches from northeastern New Jersey to coastal Maine, with heavier amounts across parts of southeastern New England. Totals of 4-8 inches are forecast from central Massachusetts to Cape Cod, Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard. The AccuWeather Local StormMax™ rainfall is 13 inches.

Improvement coming for mid-Atlantic this weekend, but slowly

Dry air from the Northeast's interior will sweep southward in the mid-Atlantic later this week, ending the rain and clearing the sky as the storm takes aim at New England and Long Island, New York.

The storm is forecast to loop toward New England, keeping its strongest winds and heaviest rain away from New York City and areas southward to Delaware and eastern Maryland. However, moderate to locally major coastal flooding is still expected around high tide through Friday.

As winds turn more northerly this weekend, coastal water levels should gradually fall across much of the mid-Atlantic. Localized flooding may persist along some back bays, where winds can keep water piled against the shoreline.

Tropical development possible near New England and elsewhere in Atlantic

"Given that the developing nor'easter will be slowly moving over the very warm water of the Gulf Stream for two or three days, the storm may take on some characteristics that would resemble a tropical storm. Such hybrid storms are called subtropical storms," Porter said. "Regardless of classification, the storm will be impactful, especially for coastal areas."

Gonzalo and Hanna are the next two names on the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season list.

AccuWeather meteorologists are also monitoring a cluster of thunderstorms moving off Africa's west coast. The disturbance could quickly organize and strengthen in the coming days, AccuWeather Lead Hurricane Expert Alex DaSilva said.

Fay regenerated over the middle of the Atlantic as a depression on Wednesday evening. Some strengthening is forecast in the short term.
