title: Albanese says OpenAI hacked Medicare and told Australia months later via email to generic inbox
description:
Prime minister says he told Sam Altman he was disappointed it had taken OpenAI ‘way too long’ to disclose breach
Anthony Albanese says an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June and the tech giant notified the government earlier this month using an email sent to a “public mailbox”.
Australia’s prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York, saying it appeared no personal information had been accessed in the AI breach.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Prime minister says he told Sam Altman he was disappointed it had taken OpenAI ‘way too long’ to disclose breach

Anthony Albanese says an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June and the tech giant notified the government earlier this month using an email sent to a “public mailbox”.

Australia’s prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York, saying it appeared no personal information had been accessed in the AI breach.

Investigations assisted by the Australian Signals Directorate were ongoing into how the agent had infiltrated Australia’s government-run universal health care system, as well as three others.

They were the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal of Services Australia.

“This situation is obviously unacceptable,” Albanese said.

“Today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident and I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.”

Albanese said both the delay and the manner in which OpenAI notified the government was disappointing.

“It took until 10 September before there was any notification at all. And the notification was an email sent to just the public mailbox,” Albanese said.

The email was sent to the public-facing email address publicdisclosures@servicesaustralia.gov.au . That inbox is checked once a day: the email was not read until 11 September.

Services Australia then reported the notification to the Australian Cyber Security Centre on 15 September.

A taskforce has been launched to explore the “legal situation” of the breach.

On Thursday, the NSW premier Chris Minns and the Victorian premier Ben Carroll both said Albanese had informed them the OpenAI breach had affected state websites – NSW’s crime agency and Victoria’s health department.

Both Minns and Carroll said it did not appear any personal information had been shared in the breach, though investigations were ongoing.

“New South Wales will be working with commonwealth intelligence agencies to get to the bottom of it,” Minns said.

Albanese said the OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia.

The portal contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending.

Albanese said the agent had accessed “public and non-public files within the portal” and, in order to do this, “engaged in writing files as well to the internal server”.

The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, said the government learned of the June breach “a couple of weeks ago” and ministers were informed last week.

Marles said the agent was non-human and he called the breach a “very serious incident”.

“What we have seen is unauthorised access in to an Australian government website and that is completely unacceptable and we have made that clear to OpenAI,” he said.

The AI agent had been given “a benign task” of researching health and medical statistics and, in doing so, had approached, as well as the Medicare portal, the three other Australian websites.

“In relation to those three, it interacted in a way that a member of the public might, so it only acted in an authorised way,” Marles told ABC radio on Thursday.

“But in relation to the medical portal of Services Australia, it sought information, information was not given, and then it effectively hacked into that medical portal and got that information anyway.

“It’s that unauthorised access which we are very concerned about. The impact is relatively minor, but the incident is very serious.”

Marles said the government had established a taskforce led by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet that was working with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute.

“We will look at what is the legal situation in respect of this and what it means to have gained an unauthorised access, albeit in an unintended way,” the acting prime minister said.

“This is a warning about the fact that artificial intelligence, which is a technology that has huge opportunity to benefit humanity, has to be developed with enormous care. There have to be guardrails and safety measures in place which are way ahead of the capability which is being developed.”

The OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and was “notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems”.

“During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” Pusateri said in a statement.

“In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.”

He said the review had found aggregate health statistics and internal file names had been accessed but there was “no evidence of patient records being accessed”.

Pusateri said OpenAI was supporting investigations and that its review was ongoing, adding it was committed “sharing what we learn as that work continues”.

Lizzie O’Shea, spokesperson for Digital Rights Watch, said the fact it took three months for OpenAI to tell the government showed that there needed to be “basic rules and standards for tech companies”.

“Artificial intelligence has potential to do some things well, but it also poses huge risks – like hacking systems that store Australians’ sensitive personal data,” O’Shea said on Thursday.

“The question is whether governments are going to let AI and tech companies run wild or whether they, on behalf of ordinary people, will put rules in place for tech companies that will promote accountability and trust.”

Independent senator David Pocock said the OpenAI hack highlighted how slow the government had been to implement AI safeguards in high-risk settings.

Pocock criticised the government’s decision to shelve plans for a National AI Safety Act, and its dilatory approach to legislating new standards.

“We have these companies warning of existential threat and hacking critical government infrastructure and the Labor government’s response is ‘We’ll get to that next year’.

“There is also a big question here around why we aren’t holding these big tech companies liable for this kind of data breach. If it was an Australian who hacked the system they’d likely be heading for jail, yet there’s no accountability for AI companies developing this technology.”

Ed Santo, former human rights commissioner and co-founder of the Human Technology Institute, told ABC radio that Australians ought to “be worried”.

“This is the first time that this has happened in any major way to an Australian database, and it’s one of the most sensitive databases that we have in government.”

OpenAI had “instructed their AI agents to go looking for information about the public health system in Australia. When the AI agents couldn’t easily find that information, they decided to break the law,” Santo said.

Describing the behaviour as “misaligned model activity” was using “a very euphemistic term”, he said.

“If we were in the bricks and mortar world, if an employee of a company went and broke the law, particularly if it broke the criminal law, then that individual would suffer serious legal consequences, but so would their company. And so we need to make sure that that is true also in this era of AI.”

fullText:
Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years in prison Wednesday, more than a year after a jury found the former Hollywood mogul guilty of sexually assaulting former “Project Runway” production assistant Miriam Haley in a high-stakes retrial.

Weinstein appeared in the downtown Manhattan courtroom in a wheelchair, his hands cuffed to his seat.

In a victim impact statement read aloud in the courtroom, Haley said Weinstein “abused his position and power,” causing a “devastating effect on my life and security.”

“It is a life sentence for me,” Haley said.

Weinstein also addressed the court, again denying the allegations against him while apologizing to “anyone I may have hurt by my actions.” He had pleaded not guilty to a charge of first-degree criminal sexual act.

“I am not a perfect person,” he said, “but I am a person who has made mistakes.” He later added: “I am not a violent man.”

Judge Curtis Farber excoriated Weinstein before handing down his sentence. “You took what you wanted by force, and you have never accepted responsibility,” the judge told the former entertainment industry kingmaker.

Farber said Weinstein’s 15-year sentence will be followed by five years of supervised release and a requirement that he register as a sex offender.

Wednesday’s sentencing came after a protracted series of trials, appeals and courtroom proceedings that have kept Weinstein behind bars since his arrest in 2018, one of the key events of the #MeToo movement.

“Today was about the survivors,” Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg said in a statement, adding: “I’m moved, as we should all be moved, by their courage and their steadfastness through what has obviously been a challenging process.”

Weinstein was originally convicted in 2020 of third-degree rape involving former aspiring actor Jessica Mann and first-degree criminal sexual act involving Haley. He was sentenced to 23 years in prison. But his conviction was overturned in 2024 by a New York state appeals court, and a judge ordered a new trial.

Weinstein was again found guilty in June 2025 of first-degree criminal sexual act involving Haley, who testified that he forcibly performed oral sex on her in his New York City apartment in 2006. The same jury acquitted him of a separate criminal sex act charge involving allegations from former model Kaja Sokola.

The jurors at Weinstein’s second New York trial could not reach a verdict on the charge related to Mann’s allegation, and a third trial on that charge also ended in a hung jury. In late June, prosecutors declined to try the Mann case a fourth time.

Weinstein was separately convicted in Los Angeles in December 2022 of rape and two counts of sexual assault related to a 2013 assault of an Italian actor and model. He was sentenced by a Los Angeles judge to 16 years in prison in February 2023.

He is set to be resentenced in L.A. after an appeals court vacated his original sentence.

The former producer and film distributor vehemently denies all allegations of sexual misconduct, insisting his sexual encounters were consensual. In all, more than 80 women have accused Weinstein of sexual assault or harassment.

Weinstein once lorded over Hollywood. Miramax, his first distribution label, released seminal independent films like “Clerks” and “Pulp Fiction.” He won an Oscar as a producer of “Shakespeare in Love.” In the early 2010s, his second distribution company scored back-to-back best picture wins for “The King’s Speech” and “The Artist.”

But his reign came crashing down in 2017 after The New York Times and The New Yorker published exposés detailing his alleged pattern of sexual harassment and assault. The first wave of accusations against him in 2017 propelled the #MeToo movement, a reckoning with sexual misconduct by powerful people in high-profile professions.

In recent years, Weinstein’s health has visibly declined, and he has faced various medical issues, including diagnoses of bone marrow cancer, kidney disease and diabetes. He has been held at the Bellevue Hospital prison ward, and he will remain there until he is sent to a state prison.

title: Mamdani and Spain's PM build ties as the left looks to counter the far right
description:
Two of the key faces of the left in elected office, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, met at an economic event in Manhattan on Wednesday, as world leaders gather in New York for the U.N. General Assembly.
Their meeting is the latest in a slate of encounters between left-wing U.S.
fullText:
Two of the key faces of the left in elected office, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, met at an economic event in Manhattan on Wednesday, as world leaders gather in New York for the U.N. General Assembly.

Their meeting is the latest in a slate of encounters between left-wing U.S. politicians and kindred figures abroad as they seek to forge ties to counter the rise of right-wing populism.

Organizers behind these formal and informal gatherings say the efforts to bring together U.S. left-leaning Democrats in office and their ideological counterparts aim to contend with the well-organized, growing international movement of populists in step with President Donald Trump's administration, as the anti-immigrant and nationalist Alternative for Germany party gains traction, and France's Marine Le Pen and her party, National Rally, lead in polls ahead of a presidential race next year.

Wednesday's event at Gracie Mansion, Mamdani's residence, was billed as focused on "building an economy for the many." Sánchez touted the success of Spain's minimum-wage increases as "proving that another economic model is possible."

"That is why the powerful fear us. Because day after day, we show that a different path is possible, and it works," Sánchez said at the event, which also included the prime minister of Barbados, Mia Mottley, and European Council President António Costa, who is a former socialist prime minister of Portugal.

Mamdani nodded to the efforts to collaborate with like-minded leaders, telling attendees, "It is truly a privilege to be able to learn from one another, emulate each others successes and develop strategies that imitate the great progress those in this room have achieved."

Heading into the U.N. General Assembly, Mamdani over the weekend hosted left-leaning mayors from Paris, Barcelona, Rome, Amsterdam, Mexico City and elsewhere for a summit on housing, migration and climate change. And he met this week with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, a social democrat in the same general tradition as Sánchez.

In April, politicians and world leaders convened in Barcelona for the first Global Progressive Mobilization conference, which was touted by organizers as an "alternative to conservative and far-right forces."

The event included prerecorded remarks from democratic socialists Mamdani and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), who revitalized that tradition in U.S. politics. But it also opened up the tent to include speeches from Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz - the 2024 Democratic vice-presidential nominee who served as a moderate "Blue Dog" Democrat in Congress - and Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut), who has embraced economic populism and urged his party to connect with voters it lost in 2024.

Giacomo Filibeck, who served on the organizing committee for April's conference, told The Washington Post that the participation of the U.S. Democrats was "instrumental" in showing how the global progressive movement can work together.

"In a nutshell, we have been rediscovering our internationalism that maybe in the past years was a bit put on the side," he added.

Democrats have long sought friends abroad. As U.S. president, especially in his first term, Barack Obama courted widespread international goodwill. But he forged a special bond with Angela Merkel of Germany's Christian Democratic Union, a center-right party at least in European terms - a different segment of the Western political spectrum than the one Mamdani is courting.

Socialists and other left-wing activists also have long organized internationally. The Sanders presidential campaign built ties to equivalent movements in Europe. The New York chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, from which Mamdani emerged, last year hosted Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the perennial French presidential candidate and founder of the hard-left party La France Insoumise.

But as energy coalesces in the left wing of the Democratic Party - with the electoral success of some candidates aligned with or backed by the DSA, Mamdani most prominent among them - the global bridge-building has taken on a new urgency.

Johan Hassel, a senior fellow and director of Global Progress Action (GPA) at the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank in Washington, said Trump's reelection in 2024 was "a game changer" that helped unify global progressives.

GPA has arranged high-level meetings between U.S. officials and center-left leaders abroad. Its most recent public convening, in Toronto this past May, included appearances by Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan), former U.S. transportation secretary and potential 2028 candidate Pete Buttigieg, and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

"The left traditionally has seen more of their differences … than their similarities. I think this is changing," Hassel said. "You're starting to see a larger democratic bloc of center-left liberals, Greens. The left that understands that something … larger is at stake."

Such politicians and movements within the U.S. and abroad, he said, "are inspiring each other" as a result of their alliances. Among the examples, he cited Mamdani's embrace of social investment in child care and housing, akin to policies long adopted by European social democrats.

Conversely, European left-wing party members made the pilgrimage to New York to canvass for Mamdani in the final weeks of his campaign. Members of Germany's anti-capitalist party Die Linke (the Left) traveled to New York to learn more about Mamdani's effort and met with his advisers.

Die Linke, whose platform is focused on lowering the cost of living and using state interventions to address the German capital's housing shortage, went on to secure a historic win in the Berlin state election Sunday.

fullText:
Jordan Love and the Green Bay Packers were able to avoid a nightmare start to the 2026 NFL season. Following their collapse against the NFC North rival Minnesota Vikings in Week 1, the Packers trailed the New York Jets 17-7 in the fourth quarter of Week 2.

Thankfully, the team was able to rally and pull out a 20-17 win over the Jets.

Nothing has looked pretty to begin the year. Love has been under constant pressure due to poor offensive line play. Through two games, however, he has been able to throw for 532 yards, four touchdowns, and an interception, although he has completed just 52.1 percent of his pass attempts.

Despite the rough start to the year, Green Bay still has faith that it can be a Super Bowl contender. One of Love's teammates has spoken out before Week 3 action on Thursday night against the Atlanta Falcons with strong words about his quarterback.

As shared by Vince Lovergine of Fox 11 News, tight end Jonnu Smith is clearly a big fan of his new quarterback. Smith was signed to a one-year deal just before the start of the regular season and has been impressed with Love thus far.

"He's a true QB1. Just a great leader," Smith said. "He's got a natural feel for alleviating a lot of pressure in the huddle. He's as talented as a thrower that I've been around."

Over the years since Love took over as the starter from Aaron Rodgers, the expectation has been that a breakout season is coming. So far, Love has failed to have the true MVP-style breakout that fans and the media have wanted to see. He has remained one of the better quarterbacks in the NFL, but he hasn't taken the full leap to "elite" status.

Love has played in 59 games throughout his NFL career. He has completed 63.7 percent of his pass attempts for 12,067 yards, 87 touchdowns, and 32 interceptions. Those numbers show why there is so much belief in Love's ability.

Only time will tell whether or not the 27-year-old quarterback can take that leap this season. The year is off to a rough start, but Love has found a way to continue making plays under pressure. If the Packers can get their offensive line issues figured out, he seems primed for a big season.

Fans will get their next look at Love on Thursday night against a Falcons team that has started the year 0-2. It will also been the home opener for Green Bay at Lambeau Field.

Hopefully, Love and the offense can get back on the right track. Moving to 2-1 would help fans forget more about the Week 1 debacle against the Vikings.

fullText:
UNITED NATIONS/DUBAI, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a speech at the UN on Wednesday that Tehran would never surrender to the US but still believes in diplomacy, a day after President Donald Trump used the same forum to threaten to "annihilate" Iran.

The duelling speeches at the ‌annual UN General Assembly in New York bookended the first shuttle talks between the United States and Iran for months, which appeared to have yielded no concessions in the public ‌stance of either side towards ending the Middle East war.

In his speech, Pezeshkian defended Iran's military actions as defensive, and insisted Iran was not seeking nuclear weapons.

In a potential new flashpoint, Iran also threatened to act against its neighbours if they ​abide by new US sanctions intended to ground Iranian civilian aircraft worldwide.

Washington has said it will impose so-called secondary sanctions against any country that allows Iranian flights after Wednesday. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state TV Iran would ensure neighbouring countries' airports could not function if they stop Iranian flights.

The annual UN gathering in New York provided the occasion on Tuesday for Iranian and U.S. officials to hold their first known indirect talks since a ceasefire collapsed in July, with Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicating through mediators on the sidelines.

"Steve and Jared had a ‌very productive meeting today with mediators of Iran," Trump said on Tuesday ⁠after his own speech. "I think there's a lot of momentum for them to make a deal. It's what we're hearing from everybody."

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran had engaged with Washington through a Qatari mediator and conveyed conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and a halt to ⁠US "acts of aggression".

Some Iranian state media initially reported that Araqchi and Witkoff had met, but Iranian officials clarified to Reuters that it was not face-to-face.

IRAN HARDLINERS RESIST DIPLOMATIC MOVES

The diplomatic contact in New York caused a backlash in Iranian media associated with hardliners.

An opinion piece run by the semi-official Tasnim news agency, associated with the Revolutionary Guards, said Araqchi was wrong to have contacts with Witkoff and Kushner, "a major gift to Trump", as Iran had ​already ​conveyed its terms.

Iranian sources told Reuters the delegation had been ordered not to meet the Americans face-to-face by the ​Supreme National Security Council, a body that includes figures selected by Ayatollah Mojtaba ‌Khamenei, the supreme leader. Khamenei has yet to appear in public since replacing his father, who was killed on the war's first day.

One Iranian journalist covering the visit told Reuters that some hardliners viewed the trip to New York itself as an insult to the memory of the slain leader, Ali Khamenei.

OIL PRICES HOLD NEAR TWO-WEEK LOW

Still, the diplomatic opening helped keep oil prices near two-week lows. Brent crude hovered around $100 a barrel after surging earlier this month when Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis launched a major offensive, threatening traffic through the Red Sea, an alternative Saudi export route.

The war, launched by Trump in February alongside Israel as "Operation Epic Fury", has lasted nearly seven months, killing thousands of people, disrupting global energy supplies and spreading to other countries in the region — particularly to Lebanon and more recently to Yemen.

An ‌interim agreement reached in June, signed by Trump and Pezeshkian, would have given Iran its main demands: lifting financial ​sanctions and unfreezing assets in return for talks on limiting its nuclear programme.

But that deal unravelled within weeks over shipping ​rules in the Strait of Hormuz, conduit for a fifth of global oil and liquefied ​natural gas before the war. Iran wants to exert control and collect fees from ships that use it, which Washington rejects.

In the latest reported attack in the ‌strait, Britain's UKMTO maritime security agency said a cargo ship had been hit ​by projectiles, causing two casualties among the crew. ​The crew had been evacuated and the ship was on fire and adrift.

Despite near-daily attacks, traffic through the strait has picked up in recent weeks. Oil producers pay shipping companies fees of as much as a quarter of a cargo's value to take the wartime risk of sailing through the strait with transponders switched off, before transferring crude to other vessels on ​the far side.

Exports from the United Arab Emirates have already recovered to ‌pre-war levels, and Saudi Arabia has sold 60 million barrels of Gulf oil for both this month and next, to be delivered beyond the strait off the coast of ​Oman.

Nevertheless, a third of Gulf oil is estimated to be missing from global supplies. Shortages have particularly hit refined products such as diesel, causing inflation, pushing up interest ​rates and hurting Trump's Republicans.

title: AOC opens up about her race and gender in weighing a possible White House bid
description:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., raised concerns during an interview published Tuesday about how her race and gender could factor into a potential 2028 presidential bid.
"Pretty candidly, I think about my identity," Ocasio-Cortez said in an interview with The New York Times.
fullText:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., raised concerns during an interview published Tuesday about how her race and gender could factor into a potential 2028 presidential bid.

"Pretty candidly, I think about my identity," Ocasio-Cortez said in an interview with The New York Times. "I’m not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina. And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities."

The progressive congresswoman said of a possible White House run, "I think about it personally."

"I am 36, I’m about to turn 37 years old — and what that means for my life," she added.

AOC, ASKED ABOUT RUNNING FOR PRESIDENT, SAYS HER AMBITION IS 'WAY BIGGER THAN THAT'

"This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?" she told the Times. "That doesn’t make it impossible, but to act as though it’s not a factor in anything ever is really a form of, like, denialism."

Ocasio-Cortez said the discussion around race and gender was often seen as a complaint or excuse.

"I often hesitate to even talk about it," she told the outlet, "because people then just register it as an excuse or a complaint."

"If you’re asking me about the things that I weigh, of course, that’s part of what I weigh," she told the Times of possibly running for president. "It’s funny because it’s kind of like, everyone else is allowed to talk about it, but I’m not?"

HASAN PIKER BRUSHES OFF DEMS WHO SEE HIM AS A LIABILITY, NAMES HIS '28 CHOICE

She argued people get defensive when gender is suggested as playing a role in electoral politics.

"I experience it tremendously — from the right and from the left," she told the Times.

Ocasio-Cortez has been generating 2028 buzz. LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman described the progressive firebrand as "pragmatic." Hoffman made the comments at Politico's Decoded Summit in September, and said former Vice President Kamala Harris would have a "very challenging path" to the nomination.

"It depends a little bit," Hoffman said when asked whether he would support Ocasio-Cortez for a 2028 run. "I think she's much more pragmatic than people give her credit for."

AOC’S PRIMARY WIN REIGNITES SPECULATION OVER 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID, SCHUMER CHALLENGE

Far-left streamer Hasan Piker said he would absolutely campaign for AOC should she decide to run in 2028.

Ocasio-Cortez topped a July poll from the University of New Hampshire Granite State. In the poll, AOC was one point ahead of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and 17 points ahead of Harris.

The polling average as of Sept. 22, according to the New York Times, has Harris leading with 27%, followed by Gov. Gavin Newsom at 16%, Buttigieg with 10%, and Ocasio-Cortez also at 10%.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Judy Pino, advisor on Hispanic issues and a Spanish-language spokesperson for Independent Women and The LIBRE Initiative, reacted to Ocasio-Cortez' remarks in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Pino said, "Whether America is ready for a Latina president isn’t the question. As a Latina, I find that framing beside the point and, frankly, insulting."

"It reduces a serious debate about the future of this country to gender and ethnicity when Americans are worried about whether they can afford groceries, buy a home, grow a business, and create a better future for their children," she continued.

Pino said Ocasio-Cortez "identifies" with democratic socialism, and argued, "we should believe candidates when they tell us what they stand for."

"For many Latinos, that debate has particular resonance. Families from Cuba, Venezuela and elsewhere in Latin America have witnessed governments embrace socialism while expanding state control and restricting economic and political freedom. Those experiences help explain why the word ‘socialism’ can carry consequences far beyond a political slogan for some Latino families,' Pino said in the statement.

Pino said Latino voters were more focused on AOC's policies rather than her gender or ethnicity.

"That's the debate America should be having: not whether we're ready for a Latina president, but whether Americans want to move this country in a socialist direction," she said.

title: Harvey Weinstein set to be sentenced for sexual assault after 6-year legal odyssey

fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — The first time Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to prison, reporters, advocates and the curious public crammed the courtroom to witness the disgraced Hollywood honcho's #MeToo reckoning.

Hours later, the world began shutting down as the COVID-19 pandemic raged. Now, after an overturned conviction and two retrials, Weinstein is set to be sentenced again on Wednesday for one of the same crimes — more than six years after his first sentencing in March 2020.

Weinstein, 74, faces up to 25 years in prison for sexually assaulting a one-time TV production assistant, Miriam Haley, at his Manhattan apartment in 2006. He has already served more than six years as his case has cycled again and again through the criminal justice system. Haley gave her account of the assault at two trials.

"The unthinkable was happening," Haley testified last year, dabbing her eyes.

Haley, who has also gone by the name Mimi Haleyi, is planning to speak at Weinstein's sentencing, her lawyer, Gloria Allred, said. Weinstein will also address the court, his spokesperson, Juda Engelmayer, said.

The Oscar-winning "Pulp Fiction" and "Shakespeare in Love" producer was originally sentenced to 23 years in prison after a jury convicted him of assaulting Haley and raping an aspiring actress, Jessica Mann, in 2013.

But New York's highest court erased those guilty verdicts in 2024, ruling that Weinstein was prejudiced by testimony from other women whose allegations weren't part of the case.

Tried for a second time last year, Weinstein was again convicted of first-degree criminal sex act for assaulting Haley. In a messy split verdict, the jury acquitted him of forcibly performing oral sex on another woman, Kaja Sokola, and could not reach a verdict on a rape charge involving Mann.

After another retrial ended in a hung jury in May, Manhattan prosecutors dropped the rape charge rather than pursue a fourth trial after Mann said she could not bear to testify again.

That decision cleared the way for Weinstein's sentencing.

Manhattan prosecutors have said they will ask for 20 years in prison — which would keep him behind bars until at least his late 80s.

Weinstein's lawyers haven't said what sentence they'll seek. He denies raping or sexually assaulting anyone. Once he's sentenced, he can appeal.

"I will be proven innocent. That I promise you," Weinstein told The Hollywood Reporter in a jailhouse interview in March.

Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate rape case in Los Angeles. A California appeals court upheld the 2022 conviction but threw out his original 16-year sentence because the judge had considered his New York convictions that were later thrown out as an aggravating factor.

After shuffling between state prison, where he tested positive for COVID-19 early in the pandemic, and New York City's notorious Rikers Island complex, the ailing Weinstein is now housed at a medical unit for jail inmates at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan.

His health issues in recent years have included chronic myeloid leukemia, diabetes and walking difficulties that necessitate a wheelchair to get in and out of court, his lawyers said. Two years ago, he underwent emergency surgery to remove fluid on his heart and lungs.

Haley, 49, is a former entertainment producer now working in advertising.

Born in Finland and raised in Sweden, she said she met Weinstein through a mutual connection and worked briefly as a production assistant on a reality competition show that he produced, "Project Runway."

Haley said she accepted an invitation to visit Weinstein's Manhattan apartment because it would have been odd to decline since she was scheduled to fly to Los Angeles the next day on his company's dime to attend a film premiere.

After she and Weinstein briefly chatted on his living room sofa, he lunged to kiss her, she testified. She said she leaped up and rebuffed him, but he grabbed her, forcibly backed her into a bedroom and sexually assaulted her, ignoring her pleas to stop.

She recalled Weinstein asking, "Don't you think we're much closer now?" after either the alleged assault or a subsequent occasion when she says she had unwanted, but not forced, sex with him.

She also recalled telling him after the second encounter, "You know you can't keep doing this."

The Associated Press does not typically identify people who say they are victims of sexual assault unless they grant permission, which Haley, Sokola and Mann have done.

fullText:
President Trump threatened the annihilation of Iran if its leaders refuse to strike a deal and framed the U.S. as conquerors of Venezuela, while promoting himself as a problem solver in his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.

“To the victor go the spoils,” Trump told the crowd, touting an oil deal with Venezuela after he launched a military operation removing its authoritarian leader in January.

The president’s remarks at the global summit kicked off a whirlwind day that included a secret meeting between U.S. officials and the Iranian delegation, with the two sides at an impasse nearly seven months into the war.

Trump also signed an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that ended a standoff over his threats to invade or annex the Arctic island.

Here are five takeaways from Trump’s appearance at the U.N.

U.S. officials met with the Iranian delegation for three hours on Tuesday, Trump told reporters, pointing to his top envoy for negotiations Steve Witkoff. The president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, also attended the meeting.

“I feel very good right now,” Witkoff said, hesitating to answer reporters’ questions about the talks.

Iranian officials have not confirmed whether the meeting took place. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi were in town for the summit.

Earlier, Trump had laid out a stark choice for Tehran in his speech to the U.N. — a deal to give up their nuclear program and reap investments from the U.S., or risk annihilation.

“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness for generations?” Trump posed to the global body and suggested Iran was waiting to see if he is in a weakened position after the midterms in November.

“I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran,” he said.

The fallout over Trump’s ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico loomed heavily over the global summit.

While a major network did not travel with Trump following the White House TV pool’s decision to boycott in solidarity with CNN, the president was pressed on the matter throughout the day.

Trump predicted a federal judge “probably will” rule in the trio’s favor after the three banned media outlets sued the administration on Monday.

“He’s not a particularly fair judge, so you never know,” Trump said, referring to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who the president nominated to the federal bench during his first term.

CNN was originally slated to travel with Trump in the pool. The ban did not stop the network from covering the president at the event in New York and even getting a question in as Trump entered the U.N.

“You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to be covering me,” Trump told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins.

The U.S., Denmark and Greenland signed a new security agreement on Tuesday that would allow Washington to build two new military bases on the Arctic island and ice out Beijing and Moscow from economic investments on the world’s largest island.

The U.S. is now planning to reestablish a military base in south Greenland in Narsarsuaq and another on the eastern side of the island in Mestersvig.

Under the deal, the U.S. would be allowed to build more military bases and “modernize and expand its activities” at the Pituffik Space Base, where about 150 U.S. service members are already stationed.

“You go back way back in the line of presidents, and almost every president at least mentioned it,” Trump said in brief remarks on Tuesday. “But most of them just mentioned it. Some really wanted to make a deal and never got done. But we’re getting it done.”

The deal came after months of tensions, with Trump at one point threatening to use military force to seize Greenland, the semi-autonomous Danish territory.

Trump sought to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence” during his remarks to the U.N. General Assembly but largely dismissed concerns about the technology and calls for global cooperation on its regulation.

The president told the body that AI would be referred to as “super intelligence” going forward in U.S. documents.

Trump went on to say using the term “artificial” makes the technology “sound fake.”

“It’s not fake. It’s actually amazing. But we have to be careful. In fact, it is exactly the opposite of what it purports,” he said.

“In other words, welcome to the new world of super intelligence — SI,” the president continued. “Let’s see if that goes. It sounds much better. It is much better, and it’s much more accurate.”

Super intelligence is already defined as a form of AI that exceeds human intelligence. It is both the ultimate goal of many frontier AI firms and the greatest worry among those warning about it running rampant.

Trump said he supports a diesel export ban, amid soaring fuel costs linked to the U.S. war with Iran. The conflict has blocked energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea, amid fighting between Saudi Arabia and Houthi rebels in Yemen.

“I’ve said let’s not send out the diesel,” the president said in response to reporters’ questions and suggested a decision on the ban could happen “fast.”

The president’s remarks underscored the drastic choices facing the administration just weeks before the midterm elections. Republicans are facing increasing odds that they could lose their majorities in the House and Senate related to Trump’s plummeting popularity over the rising cost of living and the war with Iran.

Trump’s approval rating hit an all-time low on Monday, 32 percent, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey. Almost two-thirds of Americans say the U.S. is not winning the conflict with Iran, according to a CNN poll released Tuesday.

title: Yankees must start Carlos Rodón in potential Wild Card Game 3 against Red Sox
description: New York Yankees left-hander Carlos Rodón has been pitching well as the season winds down.
fullText:
The 2026 MLB season concludes on Sunday, with all 30 teams beginning play around 3 p.m. ET. The New York Yankees are one of six clubs to officially punch their ticket to the postseason so far and are 90-66 on the year.

The Yankees' superstar outfielder Aaron Judge only managed to appear in 66 games this season due first to a broken rib and now to a strained right calf. Even with Judge missing all the time he did, New York still won a good bit without him.

The problem is that they did not win quite enough, and will likely have to play in the Wild Card round as a result. The team is second place in the American League East, five games behind the Tampa Bay Rays with six to play (three against them).

The Yankees just concluded game one of four versus the Rays Tuesday afternoon in the first game of a split doubleheader. They won 2-0 on the back of eight shutout innings from lefty starter Carlos Rodón (7-3, 2.67 ERA).

MORE: Cam Schlittler draws comparison to Dodgers legend ahead of Yankees postseason

Aug 29, 2026; Bronx, New York, USA; New York Yankees starting pitcher Carlos Rodon (55) pitches against the Boston Red Sox during the first inning at Yankee Stadium. Mandatory Credit: John Jones-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

There are still many possibilities, but in all likelihood the Yankees will host a best-of-three in the Wild Card versus their rival Boston Red Sox next week. Both teams are fairly locked into their seedings for the moment.

Games 1 & 2 should belong to right-handed AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler and elite lefty Max Fried. That leaves a starting pitcher decision for the Yankees to make regarding a possible winner-take-all Game 3.

They could have right-hander Gerrit Cole (9-9, 3.63 ERA) take the mound, as he has been mostly good following his return from Tommy John Surgery in late May. However, the hot hand lately has been their No. 4 starter in the aforementioned Rodón.

An interesting report from The Athletic's Chris Kirschner came out after game one of the Rays series. Manager Aaron Boone said that Tuesday was "potentially" Rodón's last regular season start.

The Yankees are still in play to catch the Rays in the AL East, but it is incredibly unlikely they do so. First, they would have to sweep this four-game series against them, then hope the Rays crumble in their final series of the year at the Philadelphia Phillies, all while themselves sweeping the Baltimore Orioles at home.

If Tampa Bay wins just one of these games in the Bronx, they will take the division and the AL's No. 1 seed. Boone saying "potentially" probably meant that Rodón could start Sunday versus Baltimore if the team is still alive in the division race.

Seeing as they likely will not be, that would open the door for Rodón to pitch a Game 3 versus the Red Sox. Cole has famously struggled against them in his Yankee career, and Rodón has been on fire lately.

fullText:
US president calls UK prime minister ‘a natural businessperson’ as leaders meet at UN assembly in New York

Donald Trump has asserted his relationship with the UK is “more up” with Andy Burnham than under Keir Starmer despite tensions between the two countries on a range of thorny issues including regulation of artificial intelligence, the Chagos islands and the war in Iran.

At their first face-to-face meeting, the US president praised Burnham, who sat nervously alongside him, as a “natural businessperson”, saying he thought he had “lots of assets on his side” and would be a “great” prime minister.

Burnham, who was joined in the talks by Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, and Jonathan Powell, his national security adviser, said he and Trump had built on the “good connection” they established early on, in an effort to shore up relations which had splintered over Iran.

UK officials reacted with relief that the talks appeared to have gone according to plan. But despite the warm words at the UN general assembly in New York, there were still signs of difficulties ahead.

On his way to the US, Burnham had revealed he would urge the US president to de-escalate the Iran conflict, with turmoil in the Middle East pushing up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense pressure.

Much of the summit has been dominated by geopolitical turbulence, with Trump using his speech to double down on his strategy. The president repeated his threat to “annihilate” Iran, adding he would “drive them into hell” if they did not back down and sign a peace deal with the US.

Asked later whether he had any sympathy with allies which were feeling pain over the cost of living as a result of his actions, Trump claimed that “as soon as the war is over the prices are going to come way down”.

Trump, who has suggested Iran could agree to a deal after the US midterms in November, said “people understand” the need to prevent Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon, even if that meant price hikes at the petrol pumps and in shops.

In his own UN speech, Burnham was expected to push for greater international control over AI. He revealed to business leaders that he wants a “single set of global principles and standards” to guard against rogue AI, saying the issue would be a main focus of the UK’s G20 presidency next year.

But Burnham’s ambition for the UK to be an “honest broker” between countries in that could set him on a collision course with Trump, who has called warnings about AI’s existential threat to humanity a “hoax” and gave a defiant speech in which he intensified his criticism of attempts to regulate the emerging technology.

“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” he said.

“Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge, no matter how great or how daunting that challenge may be … I’m ⁠not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than ‌the Industrial Revolution.”

Burnham is also under pressure to 

In another schism between the two countries, Trump was scathing about the UK’s deal to give away sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while paying for a lease of the military base of Diego Garcia.

“I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible. It was a terrible deal. [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous,” he said.

But he suggested that Burnham may reconsider the deal. “It’s amazing how strategic it is, and I think the prime minister is going to be looking at it,” he said, to which the UK leader nodded and said “yeah”.

However, Trump avoided commenting on the UK’s decision to ban trade with West Bank settlements, leaving it to the prime minister to answer the question. He is also understood to have agreed to a request from Burnham to bring up the case of imprisoned Hong Kong dissident Jimmy Lai in talks with China’s Xi Jinping on Thursday. British officials in the meeting suggested Lai could live in the UK.

UK officials had been somewhat nervous about the meeting, as Trump had previously dismissed Burnham as “extremely liberal” and described the former mayor of Greater Manchester as the “mayor of a town”. However, his demeanour towards Burnham was mostly cordial.

But it appeared to have gone to plan for both sides, with Trump praising US-UK relations, saying: “I think you’re up. Well, they’re more now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.

“I think right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister, Andy, I think we’re doing very well.”

Later in the press conference, Trump hit back at reporters questioning why he has banned some journalists from the White House, leading to a wider boycott by media organisations. The president claimed he had a “right to clean out fake news”.

In his UN speech, Trump promised there would be peace between Ukraine and Russia “more quickly than people understand”. After talks with Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he warned that Starmer’s rhetoric had been “too tough” towards Moscow and that London “needs to be a little bit careful”.

Many of Trump’s talking points were contradicted, however, by the UN secretary-general António Guterres, who used his speech to warn about the consequences of international conflict, climate change and AI over the past decade.

“Geopolitical divides have deepened. Inequalities have intensified. Trust has frayed. The climate crisis went from distant warning to daily reality. And artificial intelligence moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it,” he said.

Without naming Israel, he added that what followed the Hamas attack of October 2023 “was an onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza, with a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as secretary-general”.

fullText:
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 22 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed an agreement on Tuesday that permits a larger US military presence on Greenland and may resolve a standoff over the strategically located and mineral-rich island.

The agreement, signed during Trump's visit ‌to the UN General Assembly in New York, stops short of Trump's demand that the US annex Greenland as a US territory to head off the growing ‌Arctic presence of Russia and China.

But the deal does codify a greater US military presence on the icy territory, an option that emerged as Greenland leaders argued against a complete US takeover.

A text of the deal released after ​the event said the US can establish a "Golden Dome" defense system in Greenland as a shield against ballistic missile threats. The shortest route from Europe to North America runs via the Arctic island, which is the location of the northernmost US military base.

In his speech to the assembled world leaders at the UN before the signing ceremony, Trump said the agreement gives the US "permanent control over security and all other needs on that territory."

"No US adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland any more, or make sensitive investments there without our express written approval," ‌Trump said.

Trump signed the agreement along with Danish Prime Minister ⁠Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen in a trilateral ceremony after Trump gave his UN speech.

Frederiksen described the agreement as a deal that can "last forever" and said it underlines the importance of the NATO alliance and respects Greenland's right to self-determination.

Nielsen emphasized the importance of ⁠NATO in the Arctic region. "We believe that it is vital to keep NATO strong, also in the Arctic, where the alliance has a key role to play," he said.

At a press conference after the signing, Nielsen said Greenlanders must now go through a process of restoring trust with the US. Trump's threats to take the island by force had strained relations with both Greenland and Denmark.

"I believe the crisis ​is ​over now, but I don't think the conflict is over in the sense that this agreement could ​very well be used - if the Americans wish - as a platform to ‌force through further concessions," said Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen.

Greenland, a former colony and now a semi-autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, sits between the Arctic and North America and holds vast energy resources.

The US already operates Pituffik Space Base in remote northwestern Greenland. The deal opens two new military sites: Narsarsuaq, a former Cold War airbase whose population has dwindled to just a few dozen, and Mestersvig, currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish special forces unit.

"We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate location. We will be building two very major military bases," Trump said in his UN speech.

Trump's refusal to rule out military or ‌economic force to acquire Greenland triggered a diplomatic crisis in January within NATO and forced Denmark and the ​island's government into months of intensive negotiations.

The text of the agreement says it amends a 1951 defense treaty ​that had been the legal basis for the US presence.

It adds that Washington may ​seek further bases in the future, with details decided by mutual agreement. The deal has no end date, grants US aircraft and vessels broad access ‌across Greenland and its territorial waters, and bars non-NATO states from establishing ​military installations on the island.

It also restricts foreign ​investment, effectively blocking states and investors from countries outside NATO, NATO partners and the European Union from holding control or significant influence in sectors deemed particularly sensitive, including critical infrastructure and resource extraction.

The deal, which needs approval by the parliaments of Denmark and Greenland, marks a shift from Trump's earlier ambitions for an outright acquisition of ​Greenland, an island three times the size of Texas with a ‌population of only 57,000 scattered along its rugged coastline.

But it represents the first major increase in US military infrastructure in Greenland since the Cold War, when the ​US maintained 17 installations and more than 10,000 personnel there.

fullText:
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 22 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that Washington and Tehran were moving toward a settlement, while a senior Iranian official said Tehran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if the US eased military pressure and lifted its blockade on Iranian ports.

Trump's remarks came just hours after ‌he repeated a threat at the UN General Assembly to annihilate Iran if it failed to strike a deal.

Speaking after a meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the United Nations ‌in New York, Trump said: "They want to talk to us. They have been talking to us, even today they've been talking to us, and the relationship is developing.

"But we can't let them - and they understand that - we can't let them have a nuclear weapon."

He gave ​no details on the talks. No face-to-face meetings between Iran and the United States are known to have taken place since July, when an agreement on an interim deal to end the war collapsed weeks after it was signed.

Earlier, in a combative speech to the UN, Trump gave no sign of readiness to compromise. He called for Iran's complete economic isolation and said he believed a deal would be done after November's midterm elections "because it doesn't make sense for them not to. They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election."

Trump faces growing domestic discontent over the unpopular Iran war, rising energy costs and stubbornly elevated inflation.

Iran had earlier signalled a willingness to ‌revive negotiations to end their almost seven-month-old conflict, with the presidents of both ⁠countries due at the UN for the annual gathering.

The senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran had conveyed its latest proposal to Washington through mediators last week and could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to Gulf shipping within seven days if its demands were met.

IRAN SEES 'GOLDEN OPPORTUNITY' TO REVIVE DIPLOMACY

The official had earlier told Reuters that the ⁠US should "announce that it wants to resolve the issue diplomatically, make that official, and then agree on a timeline".

"The UN General Assembly is a golden opportunity for the US to return to diplomacy," the official said.

In a reminder of Iran's firm position so far, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who headed Iran's negotiating team at previous talks, said Iran would never surrender: "Trump must understand that he cannot impose his power on the Iranian people and its armed forces."

Trump was due ​to ​meet on Tuesday with leaders of the six Gulf Arab states: Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab ​Emirates.

All are keen to restore shipping through Hormuz, the conduit for a fifth of ‌global oil and gas shipments before the war, but wary of giving their longstanding rival Iran too much power.

All apart from Oman also host huge US military bases that have come under repeated Iranian attack throughout the war.

Saudi Arabia, the largest of the Gulf states, has been drawn deeper into the war this month as Iran-aligned Houthi fighters have advanced in Yemen, routing forces of the Saudi-backed government and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.

Oil markets found some relief on Tuesday after sources told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had restarted operations at its East-West Pipeline and could resume exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu within hours, albeit at reduced volumes. [O/R]

The pipeline, Saudi Arabia's main export route bypassing wartime disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, had been shut after attacks this month that Riyadh blamed on Iranian-backed groups in Iraq.

SAUDIS SEEK US SUPPORT AGAINST ‌HOUTHIS

The Houthis have driven back Saudi-supported government forces along the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at its mouth, ​and have attacked Saudi Arabia directly with missiles and drones. They are now pushing to seize the strategic heights of the Kahboub ​Mountains that overlook the Red Sea coast.

The US, which bombed the Houthis for two months last ​year, has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to rejoin the fight. The New York Times reported that Trump called off US ‌strikes against the Houthis on Sunday at the last minute.

Asked why Washington had ​held back from striking the Houthis, US Secretary of State ​Marco Rubio said: "Ultimately, if it comes down to it, the United States will always stand with Saudi Arabia and support them because we have an agreement with them to do so.

"That said, that is a very dangerous and complex conflict that pre-exists ... We have a history with the Houthis as well, and that's something we don't want to see impacted either."

On the table at the Gulf ​states' meeting with Trump is a Qatari proposal for a framework to bring ‌Iran and the Arab Gulf states into a common security architecture, regional sources said. One source said Iran was reviewing the proposal.

Speaking at the Qatar Economic Forum in New York on ​Sunday, Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said any such arrangement would need to provide security guarantees for the Gulf states and expand economic interdependence with Iran.

(Reporting ​by Reuters Gulf bureaux;Writing by Peter Graff and Kevin Liffey; Editing by Gareth Jones, Alexandra Hudson, Ros Russell)

fullText:
Former President Clinton is knocking President Trump’s plans for a triumphal arch and the efforts to put his name on the Kennedy Center, saying that global challenges would be more easily dealt with if leaders “didn’t care as much about who got the credit.”

The 42nd president delivered opening remarks at the opening of the annual Clinton Global Initiative meeting in New York on Tuesday. As he took to the lectern, Clinton quickly referenced Trump’s recent announcement that plans for a massive arch bridging Washington and Virginia would incorporate a “top grade military complex” that would be used to store drones.

“I think it’s important to take a few minutes to assess where we are now and the environment in which we are meeting,” Clinton said.

“I suppose I could take my entire allotted time to discuss the self-evident wisdom of building an Arc de Triomphe in Washington to hold all our drones,” the former president said to laughs from the audience.

“Some of this stuff — it’s hard to make up,” he added.

“Over the course of a lifetime, there are only so many real opportunities to make decisions that we know will shape our personal history and the history of those we live with and care about for a long time to come. This is one of those moments,” he said, before mentioning the Kennedy Center board’s attempts to inscribe Trump’s name on the historic Washington building.

Last week, a federal judge blocked an effort by the Trump-picked board to add the president’s name to the institution and to rename its campus after Trump.

“I personally think that the way we’ve argued about what’s going on at the Kennedy Center and all that kind of stuff — I think we’ve been majoring in the minors,” Clinton said.

“You really think 100 years from now anybody’s going to care very much about whose name’s on what building?” he asked.

“Isn’t it more important what happens in the building? And what happens outside the building?” he continued.

“I feel so strongly — as I did 30 years ago-plus when I ran for president as a virtual child — that diversity is a positive thing, not a negative one.”

“That cooperation works better than conflict, and that we could actually deal with just about every challenge we face, if we didn’t care as much about who got the credit, and we made sure that we took care of the least of these,” Clinton, 80, said.

His remarks largely focused on dealing with the development of artificial intelligence and criticizing “zero-sum thinking” by the country’s political leaders.

“I believe that on the 250th anniversary of this country, we can’t have a politics driven by zero-sum thinking: In order for me to win, you have to lose,” he said.

“Nevertheless, I do understand why so many leaders around the world have chosen this zero-sum approach. Think how richly they have been rewarded for it in every sense of the word, and this payoff has been more apparent in the United States than any other country,” the former commander in chief said.

“Some days I can hardly believe what is happening in this country that I love so much. People in charge have created one set of rules for themselves and another set for everyone else,” Clinton said, without mentioning Trump by name.

“They’ve weaponized government to settle personal scores, prosecute enemies, stamp out free speech. They’ve even made the federal government a new profit center for themselves and their allies,” he said.

“That violates the spirit and letter of the Emoluments Clause of our Constitution.”

fullText:
Green Bay Packers star edge rusher Micah Parsons may have felt a familiar sense of concern when he watched New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart suffer a knee injury on Monday.

A hit during Dart's first quarter passing attempt forced the New York Giants quarterback out of Monday's matchup with the Los Angeles Rams. Dart needed help leaving the field before the Giants announced that he would not return, and New York eventually fell 28-6. With Parsons still sidelined while recovering from his own knee injury, the Packers pass rusher took to X to respond after seeing Dart suffer the setback.

"I freaking hate injuries, man! I hate that they are a part of football!" wrote the Packers star on his post on X(formerly Twitter).

Dart is reportedly dealing with a suspected MCL sprain that could keep him sidelined for an extended stretch. Parsons can relate to the frustration of a major knee injury after tearing his ACL in Week 15 against the Denver Broncos. The 27-year-old had been enjoying a strong start to his first run with the Packers before the injury abruptly brought it to an end.

There has been speculation that the four time All Pro could make his return in Week 5 against the Chicago Bears or Week 6 against the Dallas Cowboys. However, neither possibility has been confirmed, and the Packers have yet to provide a definitive timeline for his return.

The Packers will take on the Atlanta Falcons in Week 3 at home.

fullText:
President Donald Trump gave his highly anticipated U.N. General Assembly speech Tuesday morning in front of a standing room only crowd.

However, as Trump spoke about the last six months of Iran military strikes, that country's U.N. delegates walked out of the assembly.

Trump told the gathering of world leaders in New York City said that he had a "big decision" coming up on Iran.

“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” Trump asked.

“Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?” The president continued: “Do I drive them into hell?”

Trump said he believes Tehran will “make a deal right after the [midterm] election” in November.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi are in New York for the annual meeting but didn’t attend Trump’s speech. However, their staff and delegates watched the beginning of Trump's speech then exited the General Assembly 10 minutes into his remarks. Only one Iranian delegate remained in the hall to listen to the U.S. president.

As Trump spoke about Iran, the camera panned to the lone remaining delegate from Iran, who glared stone-faced at the president.

Newsweek reached out to the Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs via email on Tuesday morning for comment.

Trump also said in his speech that he's not concerned about the war in Iran hurting Republicans in the midterm elections.

The election “doesn’t even enter my mind” when it comes to Iran, he said.

A new NBC News poll found widespread skepticism toward the conflict, with 62 percent of voters saying the war has not been worth it and 57 percent saying they would be less likely to support candidates who back it. The findings arrive amid growing Republican unease over the war's political costs, particularly in competitive midterm races.

Diesel has risen to a record $6.50 amid ongoing supply constraints from the Iran war and other global pressures, exposing a significant political vulnerability for the GOP.

Still, Trump said he’s not concerned with politics.

“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election,” Trump said of Iran. “What they don’t realize is that I’m not running. I did that already, and won in a landslide … and I’ll be here for two-and-a-half years.”

President Trump lashed out at CNN's Kaitlan Collins before his address the U.N. General Assembly in New York amid the White House ban to deny CNN, MS NOW and Politico access.

Those three news outlets are suing the president for violating the First Amendment.

Collins asked Trump as he entered the U.N. building, "Two thirds of Americans don't think the U.S. is winning the war with Iran. When will it end?"

Arriving with First Lady Melania Trump, Trump brushed aside the question and told Collins: "You should not be here covering me. You said you weren't going to cover me. You shouldn't be covering me."

After Trump's comments, Collins said on CNN that the network "never said we were not going to cover the president" and vowed that CNN would continue reporting on him despite the White House's efforts to restrict its access. She noted that the network was covering the president from the United Nations under U.N. credentials while the legal fight over White House access continues.

This is a breaking news article. Updates to follow.

The Associated Press contributed to this story.

Following their win against the New York Giants, LA Rams head coach Sean McVay made a joke about their difficult trip down under for their season opener.

The Rams earned their first win of the season against the New York Giants, beating John Harbaugh's side in a 28-6 blowout.

However, even with this return to winning ways, head coach Sean McVay still can't stop thinking about their loss at Melbourne Cricket Ground.

After the LA Rams' win against the New York Giants, Sean McVay spoke to reporters about the team's performance following a loss in Week 1.

McVay joked that losses can be lessons for the team, and suggested that he made a mistake as a coach by letting the team play their first game overseas.

"Sometimes you win, sometimes you learn. And sometimes you have a d—— coach that makes travel plans that puts you in bad spots."

Even though McVay was joking, one has to imagine that the Rams head coach had to give the green light for the Rams to play in Australia when the plans were being made.

The Week 1 fixture in Australia came as part of the NFL's global expansion plan, as the league tries to attract a bigger international audience.

Over the last few years, the NFL has held games in Brazil, England, Germany, and Australia, while boasting massive attendance figures.

But with these games moving abroad, players are forced to take long flights to different time zones. As a result, they have to take a great toll on their bodies beyond the pain they endure on the gridiron.

After their loss to the San Francisco 49ers in their opening fixture, McVay claimed that the Rams had suffered greatly because of the long travel hours.

The Rams had to travel 17 hours to reach Melbourne, and only arrived in the city 24 hours before their game, giving them almost no time to decompress physically.

Whereas the 49ers had arrived in Australia two days prior, giving them a chance to adapt to the time zone and have some practice sessions in the Australian weather.

Hopefully, McVay can continue this momentum and get the team to go on a string of wins as the season goes on.

fullText:
New York Giants fans feared the worst when Jaxson Dart went down in the first quarter against the Los Angeles Rams. Dart took a big hit after throwing a perfect pass to tight end Theo Johnson.

The Giants quarterback was visibly hurt and exited the field with a knee injury. While many assumed it would be a long-term issue, Dart has reportedly suffered a sprained MCL and could return before the end of October.

Peyton Manning and his brother Eli, who won two Super Bowls with the Giants, were both concerned about Dart after watching the incident. They will be relieved that the 23-year-old has not suffered a major injury, but it could still derail the Giants' season.

Jaxson Dart impressed in the New York Giants' Week 1 victory over the Dallas Cowboys. He threw for 230 yards and three touchdowns in one of last weekend's best quarterback performances.

The new-look Giants, led by head coach John Harbaugh, entered their Week 2 clash with the Los Angeles Rams full of confidence. However, their bubble burst almost immediately when Dart exited the game in the first quarter.

We now understand the Giants' season is not over, as Dart is likely to return within two months. But Peyton and Eli Manning did not know that when Dart was lying on the floor after taking a hit from Rams defender Byron Young.

Peyton reacted on ESPN's ManningCast: "Oh no. Oh no. No. No. No. No. That is not what we want to see. Gosh. Ugh, come on." Eli added: "Tough to watch. Hate to see that. Hopefully he's okay."

Of course, everyone wants Dart to return for his own sake, but it also matters a great deal to the Giants. They only scored six points with Jameis Winston under centre, suggesting they may not win many games in Dart's absence.
